bullets: The new Context Clash benchmark targets conflicts among coding-agent instruction files from different tools. It provides adjudicated labels for 241 file pairs from 128 repositories, sampling weights, an annotation guide, and frozen results from three detectors on 149 held-out pairs. Scripts can rebuild the benchmark because the original instruction files are not redistributed. [E001] Why it matters: If you are evaluating coding-agent governance, this adds a test for whether an agent or detector notices contradictory repository instructions across AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, Copilot, and Cursor files—not merely whether it follows one file correctly. The held-out detector results also supply a fixed comparison point. [E001] Evidence: E001. High confidence.

This captured feed shows a recurring move from checking final answers toward testing failures during execution. The new Faultline project injects tool faults into agent runs and distinguishes pass@k, whether any of k attempts succeeds, from pass^k, whether all k attempts succeed. A separate clinical system checks every proposed action and injects six fault types. [E053, E061] Why it matters: If you are choosing an evaluation for tool-using agents, final-task success can conceal unreliable retries or unsafe intermediate actions. These artifacts support adding fault injection and action-level outcomes when the product must remain dependable across repeated runs or must stop harmful actions before execution. [E053, E061] Evidence: E053, E061. Medium confidence.

The new Safety-Focused Evaluation of Scaling study separates clinical answer accuracy from safety under changing evidence conditions. Its RadSaFE-200 radiology benchmark includes clean evidence, conflicting evidence, and labels for high-risk errors, unsafe answers, and contradictions; the study applies these measures to 34 local large language models. [E043] Why it matters: If you are selecting a clinical model, this design means average accuracy alone does not cover the deployment decision. It provides separate measurements for whether a model becomes unsafe or contradicts supplied evidence when the context changes, allowing safety behavior to be compared independently of correct-answer rate. [E043] Evidence: E043. High confidence.

The new NetBench package compares four ways to add specialist knowledge—continued pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, low-rank adaptation, and retrieval-augmented generation, which supplies external documents at answer time—across eight open-weight models and three commercial model interfaces. Its 242 networking questions include source quotations, calibration outcomes, and validation results. [E009] Why it matters: If you are deciding how to build a domain-specific assistant, this creates a controlled comparison between changing model weights and supplying references during use. The attached evidence and generation pipeline also let evaluators inspect where questions came from instead of relying only on aggregate scores. [E009] Evidence: E009. High confidence.
bullets_zh: 新的 Context Clash 基准针对不同工具的编码智能体指令文件之间的冲突。它提供了来自 128 个代码仓库的 241 对文件的裁定标签、采样权重、标注指南，以及三种检测器在 149 对留出文件上的冻结结果。由于原始指令文件不再分发，因此可通过脚本重建该基准。[E001] Why it matters: 如果你正在评估编码智能体治理能力，这项基准增加了一项测试，用于判断智能体或检测器能否发现 AGENTS.md、CLAUDE.md、GEMINI.md、Copilot 和 Cursor 文件中相互矛盾的代码仓库指令，而不只是判断它能否正确遵循单个文件。留出集上的检测器结果还提供了一个固定的比较点。[E001] Evidence: E001. High confidence.

这份采集的信息流显示出一种反复出现的转向：从检查最终答案，转向测试执行过程中的故障。新的 Faultline 项目向智能体运行过程注入工具故障，并区分 pass@k（k 次尝试中是否有任意一次成功）和 pass^k（k 次尝试是否全部成功）。另一个临床系统会检查每个拟议操作，并注入六种故障类型。[E053, E061] Why it matters: 如果你正在为使用工具的智能体选择评估方法，最终任务成功可能会掩盖不可靠的重试或不安全的中间操作。当产品必须在重复运行中保持可靠，或必须在执行前阻止有害操作时，这些成果支持在评估中加入故障注入和操作级结果。[E053, E061] Evidence: E053, E061. Medium confidence.

新的 Safety-Focused Evaluation of Scaling 研究将临床答案准确性与证据条件变化时的安全性分开衡量。其 RadSaFE-200 放射学基准包含无干扰证据、冲突证据，以及针对高风险错误、不安全答案和矛盾的标签；该研究将这些衡量指标应用于 34 个本地大语言模型。[E043] Why it matters: 如果你正在选择临床模型，这种设计意味着仅凭平均准确性不足以支撑部署决策。它分别衡量模型在上下文变化时是否会变得不安全，或是否会与所提供的证据相矛盾，从而能够独立于正确答案率比较安全表现。[E043] Evidence: E043. High confidence.

新的 NetBench 软件包比较了添加专业知识的四种方式——持续预训练、监督微调、低秩适配，以及在回答时提供外部文档的检索增强生成——并在八个开放权重模型和三个商业模型接口上进行评测。其 242 道网络领域问题包含来源引文、校准结果和验证结果。[E009] Why it matters: 如果你正在决定如何构建特定领域的助手，这提供了一个受控比较，用于对比修改模型权重和在使用时提供参考资料。所附证据和生成流程还让评估者能够检查问题的来源，而不必仅依赖汇总分数。[E009] Evidence: E009. High confidence.

evidence_items.summary: This replication package accompanies the paper "Context Clash: Prevalence and Limits of Lightweight Detectors for Cross-Tool Coding-Agent Instruction Conflicts," accepted at the 42nd ACM/SIGAPP Symposium on Applied Computing (SAC 2027). The benchmark contains adjudicated conflict labels for 241 pairs of coding-agent instruction files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, GitHub Copilot instructions, and Cursor rules) from 128 repositories, repository sampling weights, and the annotation codebook. It includes frozen scores and decisions from three detectors on 149 held-out pairs. The instruction files themselves are not redistributed. Researchers can use the included scripts to rebuild the development and test inputs from the upstream dataset, reproduce the prevalence estimate and detector results reported in the paper, and evaluate a new detector against the same human labels.The benchmark labels, detector scores and decisions, derived tables, and codebook use CC BY 4.0. Project-authored code uses the MIT license. Third-party material, including the upstream dataset, keeps its original license.
evidence_items.title: Context Clash: Benchmark Data and Analysis Code for Cross-Tool Coding-Agent Instruction Conflicts

evidence_items.summary: Bulk RNA-seq simulators are widely used to develop and evaluate statistical methods, but their suitability depends on whether they preserve the properties of the data required for the intended downstream analysis. We benchmarked seven widely used simulators across five real bulk RNA-seq reference datasets using a unified framework that evaluated five complementary dimensions of simulation fidelity: marginal distribution fidelity, dependence structure, co-expression network topology, stability across repeated simulations, and differential-expression recovery. Simulator performance varied substantially across these categories, and no method consistently reproduced all properties of the reference data. Rankings differed across categories, with only moderate agreement between evaluation objectives, indicating that these measures capture distinct dimensions of simulation fidelity rather than a single underlying notion of performance. Under the network construction criteria used here, network topology was the most difficult property to reproduce consistently across simulators, whereas individual methods showed strengths in marginal distributions, dependence structure, repeated-run stability, or differential-expression recovery. Although an aggregate score provides a concise descriptive summary, it can hide meaningful differences between evaluation objectives. These results show that bulk RNA-seq simulation fidelity is inherently multidimensional and support a task-specific framework for simulator evaluation and selection, in which simulator choice is guided by the statistical and biological properties required by the downstream analysis rather than by a single overall ranking.
evidence_items.title: A multidimensional benchmark of bulk RNA-seq simulators for task-specific evaluation of simulation fidelity

evidence_items.summary: MARINA (Multimodal Annotation and Retrieval for Identification of NAtural products) predicts a molecular fingerprint from any combination of ¹H, ¹³C and HSQC NMR, tandem mass spectra ([M+H]+ and [M-H]-), molecular weight and molecular formula, and retrieves candidate structures from a set of 531,927 natural products by fingerprint similarity. This record holds the data, benchmark, trained models and source code behind the paper "MARINA: Multimodal Annotation and Retrieval for Identification of Natural Products". The source code downloads these files (download.sh) and regenerates the paper's tables from them (evaluate.sh). Files: MARINA-DB.zip: 490,003 natural products (train / val / test 441,003 / 24,500 / 24,500) with ¹H, ¹³C and HSQC NMR (experimental from JEOL CH-NMR-NP for 29,212 molecules, MestReNova-predicted otherwise) and ICEBERG-predicted MS/MS (+/−); the 531,927-structure retrieval set; unique-multiplicity and Sherlock fingerprints; NMR source flags; structure identifiers and names. MARINA-Bench-456.zip: 456 recently published natural products (test 229 / val 227) with experimental ¹H, ¹³C and multiplicity-edited HSQC from the publications, ICEBERG-simulated MS/MS, a MestReNova-predicted twin of the NMR, and the SPECTRE-clean subsets (test 205 / val 206). MARINA-checkpoints.zip: 6 trained models (the flagship and a shifts-only-HSQC variant, seeds 0, 1, 2), each with its parameters and a model card. MARINA-checkpoints-sherlock.zip: 3 models of the flagship recipe trained on the Sherlock fingerprint. marina db release s0.zip: the two models the MARINA website serves, with retrieval set, indexes and calibration. MARINA-DB-raw.zip: the inputs MARINA-DB was built from (CH-NMR-NP records, raw MestReNova and ICEBERG spectra, structures, splits), for the source code's rebuild marina db/. MARINA-code.tar.gz: source code (model, training, evaluation, table and figure sources, a prediction script for your own spectra, and the web application).

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the manuscript “An AI-Based Conversational System for Academic and Administrative Student Support in Higher Education” by Anargyros Koutsovasilis and Damianos Gavalas. AskMe is a hybrid AI-powered conversational system designed to integrate academic and administrative student-support services within a unified institutional environment. The system combines structured dialogue management, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), deterministic service workflows, and locally deployed large language model (LLM) inference. The dataset comprises experimental data and benchmark results supporting the technical and user experience evaluations of AskMe, organized into the following components: Natural Language Understanding (NLU) dataset: A Greek-language corpus comprising 267 annotated utterances distributed across six intent categories and containing 152 annotated entity spans across five entity categories, developed for academic and administrative student support. NLU learning-curve analysis: Per-epoch training and validation measurements for the baseline and optimized NLU pipelines over 50 epochs, together with the corresponding experimental configurations. Multi-seed cross-validation: Results of five-fold cross-validation conducted independently across four random seeds, including intent and entity recognition performance, classification reports, confusion matrices, confidence distributions, and error analyses. evidence_items.summary: Overview MLIRBench: A Benchmark and Dataset for Compiler and Hardware-Aware Reasoning is a research benchmark and reproducibility framework designed to evaluate the ability of large language models (LLMs) to reason about program semantics, compiler transformations, and execution behavior in the Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR). This release provides the MLIRBench codebase, benchmark dataset, experimental artifacts, and reproducibility infrastructure accompanying the paper accepted at the 2027 IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Code Generation and Optimization (CGO 2027). The benchmark consists of 1,768 original–mutated MLIR program pairs, derived from 40 curated PyTorch seed programs, including 888 linalg pairs and 880 torch pairs across five mutation difficulty levels (L1–L5). MLIRBench evaluates nine language models, producing 15,912 model reasoning records and 15,907 judged evaluation records. Release Contents This software and dataset release provides the components required to inspect, analyze, and reproduce the archived MLIRBench experiments. 1. Benchmark Dataset The dataset includes nine complementary views: Core: Original and mutated MLIR programs with semantic annotations. Master: Consolidated program, mutation, and validation metadata. Reasoning: Model-generated predictions and semantic explanations. Evaluation: Judged predictions, verdicts, and evaluation scores. Errors: Per-model error-related records. Model Arena: Model comparison and evaluation information. Performance: Program-pair runtime measurements where available. Difficulty: Mutation difficulty and aggregated evaluation information. Mutation Provenance: Transformation requirements and validation provenance. The benchmark dataset views are distributed in compressed JSONL format, accompanied by schema documentation, integrity checksums, and licensing information. Supporting downstream task datasets are provided in CSV and JSON formats. 2.

evidence_items.summary: NetBench is the benchmark, experimental framework, and analysis code behind a controlled study of how domain data becomes model competence. What this archive contains HPN-QA v5.0 — 242 generated open-ended questions (233 scored), each carrying its source evidence quotes with DOI and licence, its calibration outcome, and its validation results. The pipeline that produced it — open-access paper acquisition, PDF-to-corpus conversion, benchmark generation, and instruction-set construction. The adaptation and evaluation experiments — the direct (closed-book) and retrieval-augmented stacks, which run the same three-phase evaluation with identical judge prompts, rubric, and output schema. The judged model outputs of record and the analysis code that turns them into every number, table, and figure reported in the accompanying paper. Reproducibility. make setup && make reproduce re-derives every reported CSV, table, and figure from the committed judged outputs and exits non-zero if anything comes back different. The same target runs in CI on every push. REPRODUCING.md separates the three distinct claims this archive makes — what reproduces exactly, what re-runs approximately, and what cannot be re-acquired at all — and states the cause of each limit. Not redistributed: source PDFs, the extracted text corpus, model weights, checkpoints, LoRA adapters, and retrieval indexes. Checksums for these are recorded as provenance, not as download links. evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains post-test questionnaire data collected within a study investigating the use and evaluation of PEP ASISTENT, a pedagogically designed multimodal AI-supported learning environment developed using Google NotebookLM for the mathematics education of pre-service teachers. The study was conducted at the Faculty of Education, Catholic University in Ružomberok, Slovakia, during the summer semester of the 2025/2026 academic year, within the course Developing Arithmetic Concepts. The primary objective of the research was to investigate how students used different learning resource formats and how they perceived the suitability of the learning environment, its support for learning, and its affective benefits. The study also examined associations between the breadth and frequency of resource use, learning preferences, epistemic concerns regarding AI-generated information, and selected demographic and educational characteristics. The learning environment provided six formats of learning support: a source-grounded AI chatbot, podcasts, video overviews, flashcards, quizzes, and mind maps. Research design and sample The study employed a quantitative, non-experimental, exploratory correlational research design based on post-test questionnaire data. The final analytical sample consisted of 125 respondents, including full-time, part-time, and extension-study students. A subsample of 119 respondents who reported using at least one of the available learning formats was used to evaluate the learning environment and examine the main associations between resource use and perceived benefits.

evidence_items.summary: This study benchmarks how large language models answer fractionation counterfactuals for stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) dose constraints. Given only a published single-fraction constraint as an anchor, systems are asked for the corresponding 3- and 5-fraction limits under three conditions (explicit iso-effective conversion; a clinical vignette; and a perturbed anchor with no published counterpart). By back-calculating the implied alpha/beta of each answer and measuring exact agreement with published tables, we classify each system's strategy as retrieval-dominant, computation-dominant, or mixed, and compare failure modes (deviation from published values, unsafe-side errors, loss of internal coherence) across strategies. The reference standard is a previously compiled dataset of published SBRT dose constraints (dataset v4; 85 complete series with 1-, 3-, and 5-fraction values from AAPM TG-101, UK 2022 consensus, and HyTEC). The protocol (v1.0, frozen 28 November 2026) is attached.
evidence_items.title: Retrieval versus computation in large language model responses to fractionation changes in SBRT dose constraints: a preregistered benchmark study

evidence_items.summary: This paper constructs the projective Berry geometry on the actual relative-phase torus from the positive FBT02B prequantum line. The mixed mother form restricts to zero on a regular fibre, whereas the effective Berry ray line is the dual of the positive prequantum line. At level 24, the complete theta system gives a relative projective embedding, its quantum-geometric tensor (QGT), and the tautological Chern sign. Projective descent does not require a global normalised vector or a trivial scalar Heisenberg cocycle. The canonical positive reference Dolbeault–Dirac operator has a 24-dimensional theta kernel, no opposite-chirality zero modes, and a locally uniform gap on the smooth regular polarised family. Its heat semigroup converges exponentially to the Riesz/Bergman projector. With the specified evaluation data, this gives the heat–Bergman–QGT bridge. The scalar heat trace retains less information and does not reconstruct the projective metric. The first FBT action remains the finite-resolution heat trace of DT 6,E; its Hessian and certified spectral A3 germ are different from the reference QGT. The Serre–Riesz recovery formula is retained as an integrated Hilbert pairing. A separate pointwise pairing defines the density exported to complex periods, with the reference measure and any QGT-volume conversion specified. Full-density extension, convergence and differentiation retain the revised 06-series hypotheses and the same βd. For a supplied basepoint-free two-dimensional theta pencil, the selected ray map has degree 24 to CP1. Its ramification divisor has degree 48, and its QGT degenerates at ramification points. Thus it cannot inherit the everywhere-positive metric of the complete theta embedding. The FBT10C βd = 8 selector remains a fixed numerical benchmark with its stated certification limits.

evidence_items.summary: Reproducible offline benchmarks for electric vehicle (EV) charging require explicit transition definitions and auditable data processing. We introduce the Internet of Electric Vehicles Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IoEV-MARL) benchmark, released as two datasets from Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) runs on two real road networks: Tangier (157,071 decision-level transitions, 62 columns) and Rabat (128,008 transitions, 94 columns, with an exported candidate-station set per decision). Each covers 700 collection episodes, seven seeds, four traffic regimes and five behavioral arms (NEAREST, WEIGHTED, tabular Independent Q-Learning (IQL) and two QMIX (monotonic value function factorization) configurations). Each row is a station’s accept/reject decision on an offered EV; rejections trigger offers elsewhere. A three-layer contract separates decision-time observations, inter-decision elapsed time and outcome fields, and the extract-transform-load (ETL) protocol documents horizon censoring, missing successors and provenance. Within each network, seven-fold leave-one-seed-out Behavior Cloning on accept/reject decisions reaches balanced accuracies of 0.758 to 0.928 on Tangier and 0.69 to 0.82 on Rabat, which measure imitation rather than operational performance; single-actor offline Implicit Q-Learning provides value estimates that are not validated. In greedy evaluation, the learned policies show a higher success rate and a lower load-balance coefficient of variation (CV) than NEAREST and WEIGHTED on both networks, whereas the advantage of QMIX over tabular IQL is limited to load balance and varies with regime and seed (Tangier: 7/7 seeds under Normal traffic, 2/7 to 4/7 otherwise; unadjusted). The comparison between networks is descriptive (controller settings differ). IoEV-MARL supports offline decision-learning research; closed-loop gains of policies learned offline from it are not established.
evidence_items.title: IoEV-MARL: A Reproducible Offline Dataset and Benchmark for Electric Vehicle Charging Coordination Under Centralized and Decentralized Training

evidence_items.summary: Version 6:  Replication package for "An Initial Empirical Evaluation of Evolutionary Context Modeling for Defect Prediction under Quantified Label Noise in Enterprise Java Systems" (Turgay Taymaz and Kökten Ulaş Birant, Science of Computer Programming, accepted for publication). It contains the JML-BugDB dataset: 91,633 Java file revisions from Apache Kafka, Google Gson, and Apache Commons-IO (24,197 commits, 2002 to 2025), with SZZ labels and 14 static and process metrics. It also contains the two-rater manual audit of 398 SZZ candidate commits (commit-level precision 49.5%), all raw experiment outputs with the scripts that produce every table of the paper, and a source snapshot of the JavaMLBugDetective framework. Version 6 accompanies the post-acceptance revision of the paper. The static metrics are now computed with PMD 7.16.0 by their standard definitions (RFC and LCOM by Chidamber and Kemerer), and metrics that cannot be computed are missing values instead of fixed defaults (JML-BugDB v2.0). Every analysis involving static metrics was repeated, and missing-value sensitivity analyses and a cross-check against the CK tool were added. The source snapshot corresponds to tag v2.0.0 of https://github.com/ttaymaz/JavaMLBugDetective. Labels and process metrics are unchanged. See README.md, section "Changes in v6" Version 5: Documentation corrections only; code, data, and results are unchanged from v4. Version 4  adds the analyses of the second revision: time-ordered and cross-project evaluation, structured label noise, a drop-one process-feature ablation, a Random Forest hyperparameter check, and label-provenance analyses (results/r2 experiments/), with the per-row revision metadata and commit dates they need. All Java runners now read the datasets from a configurable data directory (JML DATA DIR). Everything in v3 is otherwise unchanged; the audit labels are the same as in v3. Version 3.

evidence_items.summary: Voice-to-face generation attempts to create a plausible facial identity from a short speech signal. The model receives a short speech from a person and the diffusion model attempts to create a plausible facial identity from it. Recent Diffusion models have improved the visual quality of faces, thus creating highly realistic faces yet they fail to create accurate identity. Thus the aim of this work is not to propose another face generator but to research and investigate why the current voiceto- face diffusion models fail to create accurate faces from a short speech signal. The proposed study treats the face generation pipeline as a sequence of potentially lossy transformations: speech representation learning, cross-modal identity alignment, identityconditioned diffusion, and final face synthesis. The failureanalysis framework is proposed using the following: identity similarity, retrieval accuracy, demographic and acoustic subgroup analysis, perturbation and counterfactual experiments, and explainability methods such as Integrated Gradients and SHAP. The methodology further examines whether identity information is lost during speech-to-face alignment or subsequently distorted by the diffusion process.Public audio-visual datasets like Vox- Celeb2 and AVSpeech, together with HQ-VoxCeleb used in recent more successful models are considered for controlled evaluation. The expected result of this work is a characterization of failure analysis that is acoustic, alignment, demographic, and generative failure modes , further providing evidence and analysis on why a diffusion based voice-to-face model should not be trusted to reproduce speaker identity.
evidence_items.title: Voice2Face-Diffusion: A Benchmark Dataset for Failure Analysis of Diffusion-Based Face Generation

evidence_items.summary: Protein engineering often requires improving one property while preserving others across multiple regions or molecular states. An aggregate score can reveal a poor design yet offer little guidance about which decision to revise. We introduce DASTevolve, which represents a design task as two linked abstract syntax trees. The functional tree specifies objectives and state relationships, and its links to the structural tree identify where edits are permitted for each objective. A large language model (LLM), as inspired by the recent works on coding agents, proposes program revisions from evaluation feedback, and a sequence optimizer searches within the compiled constraints. In an α-synuclein binder-design ablation with 2,000 candidate evaluations per method, the best feasible DASTevolve candidate achieved an ESMFold binder-chain confidence score (pLDDT) of 63.1, compared with 52.9 for the strongest of three controls, a single-tree controller. In an enzyme-scaffold redesign comparison with one retained trajectory per condition, four of the first ten accepted proposals under region- and objective-specific feedback revised editing rules or functional mappings. Neither control trajectory showed such revisions over the same window. Additional case studies illustrate how the representation accommodates antibody design, peptide selectivity, and ligand-responsive design. Together, these results show how an LLM can use evaluation feedback to revise an executable protein design program while preserving a traceable link from functional objectives to individual sequence edits.
evidence_items.title: DASTevolve: Evolving executable protein-design programs with large language models

evidence_items.summary: Nationally representative surveys track public opinion, yet they ask only a limited set of questions each year, limiting their potential to capture historical changes. To fill this gap, the authors develop a large language model (LLM)–based framework for predicting missing responses in repeated cross-sectional surveys by incorporating embeddings for questions, respondents, and survey periods. The authors introduce two new applications of LLMs to survey research: retrodiction (predicting year-level missing opinions) and unasked opinion prediction (predicting entirely missing opinions). Using data from the 1972 to 2021 General Social Surveys (GSSs), the LLM-based models perform strongly in retrodicting masked GSS opinions through cross-validation and public opinions measured by other organizations in years when the GSS did not ask these questions. These capabilities make it possible to recover missing trends and pinpoint when public attitudes changed, such as the rising support for same-sex marriage. However, performance remains modest for unasked opinion prediction. The authors show when their models outperform established benchmarks, examine which opinions and respondents are more predictable, and evaluate whether their approach reduces LLMs’ tendency to homogenize predicted responses. This study demonstrates that LLMs and surveys can mutually enhance each other: LLMs broaden survey potential, and surveys calibrate LLMs for simulating human opinions.

evidence_items.summary: Dataset overview This dataset provides a qualified, traceable and reproducible collection of coupled aero-hydro-servo-elastic OpenFAST simulations of the NREL 5-MW reference wind turbine mounted on the OC4-DeepCwind semisubmersible floating platform. The dataset comprises 1,280 numerical simulations organized into 256 Sea-State Groups, defined by a systematic combination of 16 nominal significant wave heights and 16 peak wave periods. Each group includes five simulations corresponding to below-rated wind speeds of 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 m/s. The dataset is intended to support floating offshore wind turbine research, numerical benchmarking, wind–wave response assessment, surrogate modelling, machine learning, sensitivity analysis and reproducible comparisons of turbine and platform responses under combined environmental loading. Dataset contents The release includes: 32 ZIP archives containing the original OpenFAST numerical outputs, with a combined size of approximately 145.94 GB; structured simulation metadata and persistent identifiers linking environmental conditions, Sea-State Groups and individual numerical realizations; qualification criteria, classification tables and associated decision records; predefined group-level development, cross-validation and frozen hold-out partitions; documentation of the numerical configuration, simulation procedures and reproducibility workflow; supporting numerical sensitivity analyses and diagnostic assessments; archive integrity records, file-level traceability information and checksum manifests; scripts for validating the consistency of the released metadata. Qualification framework A documented qualification framework is applied to the simulated sea states to distinguish their suitability for different downstream applications. The classification considers wave-steepness constraints, the adopted engineering admissibility criterion and numerical output completeness.
evidence_items.title: A Qualified, Traceable and Reproducible FAIR OpenFAST Dataset for the NREL 5-MW/OC4-DeepCwind Floating Wind Turbine Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Educational materials usually have structures that create barriers to accessibility for learners with varied linguistic, cognitive, and educational backgrounds. Simplifying such texts can improve comprehension and enable inclusive learning by communicating core content in a more accessible and reader-friendly manner. Generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs), can help with its ability to dynamically adapt text to different literacy levels while preserving contextual meaning. This study systematically evaluates six state-of-the-art LLMs—GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3.5 (proprietary), and LLaMA 3.2, Qwen 2.5, DeepSeek-V2 (open-weight). ASSET, a general-domain dataset, was used for this evaluation. Its lexical and syntactic variety provides a robust proxy for educational simplification. We assess models across four dimensions: simplification quality (SARI), readability (FKGL, Gunning Fog), semantic fidelity (BERTScore-F1, Levenshtein distance), and surface similarity (BLEU, ROUGE-L). The study addresses three research questions: (1) How effectively do LLMs simplify texts? (2) What trade-offs exist between readability, fluency, and meaning preservation? (3) Which evaluation metrics best align with human judgment? Results show that GPT-4o-mini achieved the highest overall simplification quality, with a leading SARI score of 48.2 and a BERTScore-F1 of 0.8746, indicating strong semantic alignment and practical simplification. GPT-4o followed closely, excelling in alignment with reference texts. In contrast, open-weight models like Qwen 2.5 prioritized readability (FKGL = 9.1) but introduced more substantial changes (Levenshtein distance = 80.5), often at the expense of meaning retention.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Text Simplification: Implications for Educational Accessibility

evidence_items.summary: Electronic health record foundation models are evaluated using heterogeneous targets, vocabularies, and adaptation procedures, preventing systematic characterization across model families. We introduce EHRMENEIA (https://ehrmeneia.upc.edu/), a benchmark that provides a multidimensional evaluation framework for next-event prediction, multi-horizon event occurrence, trajectory fidelity and few-shot representation transfer. EHRMENEIA preserves each model's native vocabulary and temporal representation while mapping clinical outputs to shared evaluation objects. Applied to two released clinical checkpoints and two synthetic demonstrations, the framework exposed substantial differences not only in performance but in the clinical questions that could be evaluated from each model--dataset interface. EHRMENEIA introduces a view of benchmarking in which the supported clinical evaluation domain is identified before performance within that domain is interpreted. The framework therefore shifts foundation-model benchmarking from scalar ranking toward characterization of what can, and cannot, be inferred from model outputs.
evidence_items.title: EHRMENEIA: A Benchmark for Foundation Models on Longitudinal Electronic Health Records

evidence_items.summary: Gene network (GN) inference plays a critical role in understanding gene relationships and their roles in biological functions and diseases. Existing single-cell GN inference methods often rely on limited data from individual studies. Single-cell foundation models, pretrained on large and diverse datasets, provide a range of gene-gene association signals that offer a promising basis for GN inference. However, it remains unclear which GN properties these signals capture and how they compare with domain-specific methods. To address this gap, we introduce GNEval, a unified benchmark for evaluating pretrained model derived gene associations for network inference. We benchmark 21 gene representations and association scores from 11 models, including static gene embeddings (S), contextual embeddings (C), and gene-gene attention scores (A). GNEval assesses inferred networks based on their consistency with functional and perturbational evidence, including 14 Perturb-seq datasets across diverse cell systems, perturbation types and data sizes. The results reveal substantial heterogeneity across evaluation tasks and models. Rankings based on Gene Ontology and Perturb-seq evidence were nearly uncorrelated (Spearman ρ = −0.05). Context-independent representations showed a substantial advantage in recovering functional relationships (ΔAUROC = 0.13), whereas context-dependent gene associations improved recovery of perturbation-associated differential expression relationships by 3.8×. The domain-specific method achieves relatively strong performance on both evidence types, offering a better balance across the two evaluations than most foundation-model-derived networks. Overall, gene representations and association scores show task-specific strengths, highlighting the need for task-aware selection and integration with domain-specific methods.
evidence_items.title: GNEval: A Context-Specific Benchmark for Gene Network Inference with Single-Cell Foundation Models

evidence_items.summary: Large-scale kinetic models predict how metabolism responds to genetic and environmental perturbations, but building them at scale is limited by the scarcity of experimentally determined enzyme kinetic parameters. Generative machine learning has been proposed to address this bottleneck, yet prior work has each introduced a single, bespoke architecture, leaving open which generative paradigm suits this problem and why. We introduce a benchmark suite for generative modeling of high-dimensional enzyme kinetic parameter sets: labeled datasets of kinetically feasible Escherichia coli models paired with a mechanistically grounded evaluation harness that scores generated ensembles on dynamical stability and agreement with experimentally observed phenotypes, rather than statistical realism alone. Using it, we compare three standard architectures at matched capacity, a conditional variational autoencoder, a Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty, and a RealNVP normalizing flow, each under two conditioning schemes (a discrete high/low label and a continuous, graded key-performance-indicator target), across a difficulty ladder from one mutant phenotype to a stringent class of nine reproduced jointly. Two findings stand out. The architectures trace a consistent concentration-exploration trade-off, the VAE concentrating, the flow exploring and extrapolating, the GAN in between, but this ordering is overturned at high stringency by the conditioning scheme: at the joint class, continuous targets reach 33 to 117-fold enrichment over random sampling for every architecture, whereas discrete labels stay at 1.3 to 15-fold. Beyond the comparison, the suite is an accessible, mechanistically validated reference task for groups outside the kinetic-modeling community to benchmark their own generative algorithms.
evidence_items.title: A Benchmark for Generative Modeling of High-Dimensional Enzyme Kinetic Parameters of Metabolic Networks

evidence_items.summary: Virtual cells, computational models that predict how cellular state changes under genetic, chemical or environmental perturbation, are increasingly built, queried and revised by artificial intelligence (AI) agents rather than by human modellers alone. Here we argue that the consequential change is not a further increase in the capacity of any single model but the explicit implementation of an operator layer: the decisions about which model to trust, which evidence to add and which experiment to run that human modellers have always made implicitly. We define an agentic virtual cell as a coupled system of a predictive cell model, an agent policy, an evidence ledger and a laboratory interface, and we distinguish four couplings through which agents and virtual cells interact: agents use models as instruments, build models, plan with models as world models and learn from models as verifiers. Drawing on the 2025 Virtual Cell Challenge, recent benchmark disputes and the first agent-built and agent-operated systems, we show that current performance limits arise jointly from model capacity, coverage of biological context and evaluation design, and that agents can relieve the second but cannot, by orchestration alone, create causal identifiability. We propose a two-tier evaluation of model outputs and agent trajectories and state five falsifiable predictions for the next five years.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Virtual Cells (AVCs): From Cell Models to Auditable Discovery Systems

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Single-image super-resolution (SISR) can enhance the spatial resolution of aerial and satellite images, but generative models sacrifice pixel fidelity for perceptual realism. We compared regression (EDSR, RRDBNet), adversarial (ESRGAN) and diffusion (SR3-style) architectures under one ×4 protocol on UC Merced, with cross-dataset testing on AID, paired statistics, a frozen land-use classifier and robustness tests over training seeds, diffusion training length and realistic degradations. Regression achieved the highest fidelity (RRDB-PSNR 29.00 dB PSNR-Y), whereas ESRGAN (LPIPS 0.155) and diffusion (0.195) reduced perceptual distance relative to regression (0.294) at a fidelity cost; this ordering held on AID and across training seeds. A classifier trained on original images reached 98.6% on them and 86.2% on bicubic upsampling; its accuracy on generative outputs was statistically indistinguishable from the originals (98.8% and 98.1%) and on regression outputs slightly lower (96.4–96.9%). Doubling diffusion training did not help. Realistic blur, noise and compression reduced accuracy on all super-resolved outputs to 82–84%; short degradation-aware fine-tuning restored ESRGAN to 94.5%. Diffusion inference was about 73 times slower than ESRGAN. Fidelity and task utility favour different families, so remote-sensing super-resolution should be evaluated on both, under realistic degradations.
evidence_items.title: Regression, adversarial and diffusion architectures for single-image super-resolution of remote-sensing imagery: a statistically controlled benchmark with downstream land-use evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract. Consumer large language model (LLM) interactive-fiction products are marketed on narrative continuity but are almost always evaluated on prose quality. This preprint separates the two. We report a fixed-protocol, single-day, zero-dollar, zero-card benchmark of ten consumer web products conducted on 15 November 2026, built around a 15-turn retention probe: an identical fact ("My cat's name is Marmalade.") is planted at turn 2 and queried verbatim at turn 15. Four of ten products reached turn 15; three of those four (75%) recalled the fact, while one fluent, on-persona session silently lost it. Four further products were right-censored before the probe could be administered by signup walls, paid-trial gates, or non-persistent sessions, and two were untestable under the protocol. We argue that the dominant continuity risk in this category is not local prose quality but silent state drift - a failure that leaves the immediate utterance fluent while the narrative record is wrong - and we introduce a five-mode taxonomy of it. As a constructive response we document branching-story-kit, a 207-line, zero-dependency deterministic story-state kernel (JSON scene graph, additive/assigning reducer, guard predicates, invariant validator, and a turn-stamped memory log) released under MIT with a 21-test conformance suite. We close with preservation risk: in the companion late-2026 availability dataset, two companion applications were removed from the iOS App Store, decoupling reader continuity from reader investment. Data and code availability. All measurements, instruments, and code are open and persistently identified. Primary dataset: Harvard Dataverse, https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/YEBHQR ; CERN Zenodo mirror, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24511974 . Software (branching-story-kit v1.0.0, MIT): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24514910 ; source at https://github.com/ouba-studio/branching-story-kit ; JSR package at https://jsr.io/@ouba-studio/branching-story-kit .
evidence_items.title: State Drift in Consumer LLM Interactive Fiction: A 15-Turn Empirical Benchmark Across 10 Platforms and a 207-Line Deterministic Story-State Kernel

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Clinical large language models (LLMs) are commonly scaled by increasing model size, context length, retrieval complexity, or inference-time compute, on the assumption that higher accuracy implies safer behavior. In medicine, where a few confident or evidence-contradicting errors can outweigh average performance, this assumption may be incomplete. We introduce Safety-Focused Evaluation of Scaling (SaFE-Scale) and instantiate it on RadSaFE-200, a 200-question text-based radiology multiple-choice benchmark with clinician-defined clean evidence, conflict evidence, and option-level labels for high-risk error, unsafe answer, and evidence contradiction. Thirty-four local LLMs were evaluated across six deployment conditions spanning closed-book, evidence-grounded, standard and agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and max-context prompting. Clean clinician-written evidence, used as an upper-bound, produced the strongest joint gain, raising mean accuracy from 73.5% to 94.1% and reducing high-risk error from 12.0% to 2.6% and dangerous overconfidence from 8.0% to 1.6%. Standard and agentic RAG, max-context prompting, and inference-time compute improved selected metrics but did not reproduce this safety profile. Clinically consequential errors concentrated in a small subset of questions, and variance decomposition placed deployment condition above model family on every safety metric. Within this evaluation, clinical LLM safety did not track accuracy scaling but emerged as a deployment-level property.
evidence_items.title: Safety and accuracy diverge across deployment conditions in clinical large language models

evidence_items.summary: This record contains the complete analysis code and the numerical source data for all results figures of the manuscript "Do Explanations of Brain-Inspired EEG Decoders Agree with Band-Power Discriminability? A Leakage-Controlled Evaluation of Explainable AI on a Motor-Imagery Dataset" (Okmi, Shafei and Alhazmi; Jazan University). The manuscript was submitted to Biomimetics (MDPI), manuscript ID biomimetics-4702058. The code reproduces every number in the manuscript and its Supplementary Materials from the public BCI Competition IV dataset 2a (left- versus right-hand motor imagery, nine participants). It covers: training EEGNet, ShallowConvNet and CSP-LDA under session-to-session, within-session, artefact-free, tuned and cross-participant settings; five post-hoc attribution methods (saliency, gradient × input, Integrated Gradients, GradientSHAP, channel occlusion) and EEGNet's built-in activation patterns; the band-power discriminability reference and its reproducibility, a signal-power baseline and a class-specific ERD check; channel-deletion faithfulness, cascading parameter randomisation and seed-stability analysis. Contents: prep.py, lib.py, train all.py, hpo.py, hpo select.py, cross.py, xai.py, stats.py, export figdata.py: the analysis pipeline. Run order and requirements are in README.md. figure source data/: CSV files holding the numbers behind each results figure. plot figures.ipynb: the plotting notebook used to generate the figures from these CSV files. The raw data are not redistributed here. The EEG signals are available from https://github.com/bregydoc/bcidatasetIV2a and the true labels from https://www.bbci.de/competition/iv/.

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains the per-image evaluation results of a quantum-safe framework for academic certificates that combines a five-dimensional hyperchaotic cipher with dynamic DNA coding and a quantum-walk permutation, Fibonacci-spaced LSB embedding, an SLH-DSA seal and anchoring on the QRL Zond ledger. Version 2 replaces Version 1 and reports the results on the QVISTA dataset of 1,500 certificate images (10 templates × 10 certificates × 3 resolutions × 5 formats). For every template, the files contain the statistical security of the cipher images (entropy, χ², adjacent-pixel correlation, NPCR and UACI with the Wu tests), the quality of the stego images (MSE, PSNR, SSIM, BER), execution time and memory, robustness against eight manipulations, structural steganalysis (χ² attack, RS and SPA), an ablation study, re-implemented baseline ciphers, key sensitivity and NIST SP 800-22 randomness tests. The aggregated values, the evaluation and plotting scripts, a Google Colab notebook and the result figures of the article are included.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation Results of a Quantum-Safe Certificate Framework: Hyperchaotic DNA–Quantum-Walk Encryption, Fibonacci-LSB Embedding and Post-Quantum Sealing (QVISTA dataset)

evidence_items.summary: This archive contains the derived dataset, the analysis scripts, all machine-readable result files and the vector figures that reproduce every number and figure of the manuscript "How Much Density Functional Theory Does a Screening Agent Need? A Descriptor-Tier Benchmark for Exfoliation-Energy Prediction of Layered Materials" (Siyuan Zhou, Nanyang Technological University), submitted to Materials (MDPI) in November 2026. Contents. data/dataset.csv is a 748x44 table, one row per two-dimensional entry of the public JARVIS-DFT release, holding the exfoliation-energy target (meV per atom), the OptB88vdW band gap, the formation energy, the relaxed lattice parameters and the composition-derived descriptors. data/results/ holds the cross-validation table, the out-of-fold predictions, the conformal, triage, family-transfer, policy and bootstrap outputs, and the cross-database label-check table. data/ .py are the scripts that produce the dataset, the results and the figures from the public sources; figures/ holds the submitted vector figures. A README maps each claim in the manuscript to the file that produces it. Provenance. The 748 entries are the two-dimensional subset of JARVIS-DFT (Choudhary et al., npj Comput. Mater. 2020; https://jarvis.nist.gov); no value in dataset.csv was recomputed here, the table is a filtered and renamed view of the public release. The cross-database check uses the Materials Cloud two-dimensional database (Mounet et al., Nat. Nanotechnol. 2018; archive https://doi.org/10.24435/materialscloud:az-b2); only derived comparison values are redistributed here, the raw snapshot is fetched from the public REST endpoint. Reproducibility. Python 3.9+ with numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn and matplotlib. Scripts run from inside data/; random seeds are fixed and the repeated nested cross-validation uses 5 folds x 2 repeats (10 fits) with an inner 3-fold grid search, so reruns reproduce the reported values to the last printed digit. Licences.

evidence_items.summary: Code and data for: "The HPV E1 Arginine Triad in E1-E2 Complex Formation: Spatial Architecture of the E2-Binding Cleft and Computational Design of Peptide Inhibitors" Overview This archive contains the computational pipeline, structural models and processed analytical data for the manuscript above (PLOS ONE, PONE-D-26-41023). It provides the scripts and configurations needed to reproduce the dual-scale molecular dynamics, MM/GBSA thermodynamic scoring and trajectory analytics used to evaluate the designed peptide binders. What is new in this version Relative to the previous deposit: production trajectories are continuous 100 ns runs per system, replacing the 50 ns design. Four negative controls were added under the same short-screen protocol as the candidate screen, comprising two designs discarded at structural filtering (Binder 12, Binder 9) and two composition- and charge-matched Binder 8 scrambles (Scramble 1, Scramble 2), together with computational alanine scanning of E1 R20, R27, R195 and R199. Thermodynamic statistics were recomputed directly from the 50 per-run MM/GBSA values, and the stability, DCCM and DRN figures were rebuilt from the 100 ns trajectories. All four controls score less favourably than both the native complex and every advanced candidate, indicating that the endpoint score responds to sequence arrangement rather than composition alone. Predicted structural confidence is a partial confound across the control set, and no experimental binding data exist. See REVISION NOTES.md for scope, caveats and data locations. Repository organization 00 Generative Design/ — AlphaProteo generation parameters and the raw sequences of the generated candidates. 01 Structural Predictions/ — AlphaFold 3 predicted geometries (.cif) and confidence metrics (.json) for all 14 candidates and the native 1TUE complex.

evidence_items.summary: This open empirical benchmark dataset documents 36-month Total Cost of Ownership (TCO), workflow execution overhead, and multi-agent LLM latency across leading 2026 enterprise ecommerce automation platforms (n8n Self-Hosted vs Cloud, Make.com, Relevance AI, and Gorgias AI Agent) and production orchestration frameworks (LangChain / LangGraph, LlamaIndex, and CrewAI). 1. Ecommerce Automation Economics: Per-Ticket vs Execution Pricing (2026) Mid-market direct-to-consumer and B2B ecommerce operators crossing 15,000 monthly orders encounter sharp unit-cost divergence across automation architectures. Per-resolution helpdesk AI agents (Gorgias AI at $0.90–$1.00/ticket) scale linearly with seasonal Q4 ticket surges ($148,000–$192,000 over 3 years at 25,000 tickets/month), whereas self-hosted n8n nodes backed by direct LLM API calls reduce 3-year software + compute TCO to $22,400–$36,800 for engineering-capable operations teams. Visual iPaaS platforms (Make.com and Relevance AI) sit in the $54,000–$114,000 range depending on polling frequency and multi-step reflection loop depth. Interactive 3-year TCO scenario modeling (ticket deflection rate, average LLM token depth, and engineer maintenance hours) is published in the live AI Agents for Ecommerce Automation (2026): n8n vs Make vs Relevance AI vs Gorgias TCO Calculator. 2. Multi-Agent Orchestration Latency & Token Overhead For engineering teams building custom Python/TypeScript multi-agent workflows, deterministic graph-state control (LangGraph/LangChain) excels at human-in-the-loop refund approvals, LlamaIndex leads on hybrid BM25 + dense-vector SKU catalog retrieval accuracy, and CrewAI accelerates role-based merchandising pipelines when strict iteration caps prevent runaway token loops. Full latency and token-overhead benchmarks are available in the LangChain vs LlamaIndex vs CrewAI (2026) Production Latency & Multi-Agent Benchmark. 3.

evidence_items.summary: Some agent-based policy experiments score an allocation rule against agents whose presence the rule changes: households on a waiting list, workers in the labour force, families registered this month. This paper shows that a ratio against such a moving benchmark can rise while allocated value falls, and that two policies can swap ranks when access is counted over open arrivals instead of a fixed entry cohort. Proposition 1 gives exact conditions for the value reversals; Proposition 2 splits an open-run unserved rate into completed-cohort access and late-arrival censoring. In a two-class triage queue both reversals occur in all 50 paired runs. In a housing model with institutional buyers, a duty on institutions lowers allocated value yet raises the moving-benchmark ratio above about a 2 percent offer discount. In PolicySpace2, a published model of Brazilian cities, monetary aid assists 184 times as many households a month as property acquisition but 2.5 times as many families, while in each of three settings property acquisition has the lowest share of its entrants recorded below the poverty line at month 24. In LivSim, the estimated third-year change in mortality disparity shifts by 5.5 percentage points under common status-quo denominators. In 25 published policy experiments from two journals, seven use denominators that the policy can move. The paper ends with five reporting rules and a standard-library script that checks paired comparison records. Files. The paper and its online supplement (PDF); methods v8 0 replication package.zip with the scripts, saved outputs, 256 exported comparison records, the denominator survey (protocol, coding sheet and journal frames), the manuscript sources and a README with the commands that reproduce every table check; ps2 monthly logs.zip with the 200 monthly PolicySpace2 logs for Brasília at 1% and 2% of the population and Fortaleza at 1%; and livsim synthetic inputs.zip with the synthetic LivSim inputs.
evidence_items.title: When the Benchmark Moves with the Policy: Efficiency and Access in Agent-Based Allocation Models

evidence_items.summary: Digital twins and multi-agent artificial intelligence are increasingly proposed together for intelligent energy management — coordinating distributed energy resources, balancing virtual power plants, and orchestrating demand response across many independently-acting components — yet no reproducible benchmark evaluates this specific combination under a governed, versioned architecture. This paper introduces BQEB (BIO-Quantum Energy Brain) TwinAgentBench, the fifth module of the BQEB research program. Consistent with the architecture established across Papers 1–4, TwinAgentBench introduces no new architectural layer: it registers as the fifth module of the existing Benchmark Evolution Layer, alongside ForecastBench, SecBench, FoundationBench, and ExplainBench. The framework specifies eight benchmark tasks spanning digital twin state estimation, twin synchronization and fidelity assessment, multi-agent coordination, consensus formation, adaptive control, fault recovery, human-in-the-loop intervention, and open-world adaptation, formalized as a 6-tuple B = (W, A, T, C, E, R) over twin models, agent ecosystems, tasks, inter-agent communication, evaluation, and reproducibility artifacts. Eleven component metrics — spanning twin fidelity, synchronization accuracy, temporal consistency, agent coordination, consensus stability, communication efficiency, adaptation quality, fault recovery, safety preservation, human intervention quality, and deployment readiness — are specified for aggregation into composite benchmark indices, following the same evidence-tier discipline established in Papers 3 and 4. Beyond specification, this manuscript reports a minimal executed pilot — a small, fully-disclosed toy implementation of three of the eight tasks, run end-to-end to confirm the component metrics compute from real trajectories and discriminate between baseline agents as intended.
evidence_items.title: BQEB TwinAgentBench: A Reproducibility-First Benchmark for Digital Twins and Multi-Agent AI in Trustworthy Energy Systems

evidence_items.summary: This dataset corresponds to the research paper Inhibitory Activity of Seven Foliar‑applied Herbicides against the Growth of Ipomoea purpurea and Their Crop‑safety Evaluation (Meng Zhen, Deng Fengzhi, Wang Shen, et al., World Pesticides , 2025, 47(4): 58‑62). It contains only the full‑text of this paper and its associated data. The research focuses on the herbicidal activity of foliar‑applied herbicides commonly used in maize fields against the invasive weed Ipomoea purpurea , as well as their safety to maize. This is an experimental research paper. Data are stored in pdf, xlsx and docx text files. The results are mainly presented in figures and tables, including Table 1 (tested herbicides and manufacturers, covering seven herbicides and their recommended application rates), Table 2 (growth‑inhibitory activity of foliar‑applied herbicides against Ipomoea purpurea , including GR₅₀, GR₉₀, regression equations and correlation coefficients), and Table 3 (selectivity index of foliar‑applied herbicides for maize and Ipomoea purpurea , including GR₁₀ and selectivity index (SI) of two maize varieties, Xianyu 335 and Nendan 8). The dataset covers greenhouse potted whole‑plant bioassay experiments. The tested materials include Ipomoea purpurea at the 3‑ to 4‑leaf stage and maize at the 3‑ to 5‑leaf stage. Each of the seven foliar‑applied herbicides was set with five dose gradients plus a water control, with four replicates per treatment. Above‑ground fresh weight was surveyed 28 days after herbicide application.

evidence_items.summary: Conventional  large-language-model  (LLM)  workflows are often organized as linear prompt response chains in which actions are selected  implicitly and failures are handled manually. Such  workflows become fragile and hard to govern when  tasks involve dependent operations, external tools,  code execution, persistent context, or recovery from  failures. This paper presents an autonomous agent  framework for goal-oriented multi-task execution,  designed and implemented as an integrated, modular  prototype whose structure follows the agentic intelligence taxonomy of Acharya, Kuppan and  Divya [7]. The system has six layers: (1) a FastAPI based interface layer; (2) a planning layer that  decomposes a goal into a Directed Acyclic Graph  (DAG) of sub-tasks and a Dynamic Replanner that  rewrites the unexecuted part of the graph after  repeated failures; (3) an execution engine with tools  for web search, sandboxed code execution, report  generation and external REST API calls; (4) a dual  memory of per-run episodic traces and persistent  SQLite storage with keyword-based retrieval; (5)  Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) and Human-on-the Loop (HOTL) governance with an append-only  Explainable-AI (XAI) audit trail; and (6) an  evaluation layer. Sensitive operations are held in an  AWAITING APPROVAL state until an operator  decides, with real-time WebSocket telemetry to a  dashboard. The prototype was exercised on 29 goal  workflows, which produced 216 audit records. We  define four evaluation metrics, describe a baseline  and ablation protocol, and discuss limitations,  including the small test set and the lack of a baseline  comparison in the present study.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI-Based Autonomous Agent for Goal-Oriented Multi-Task  Execution

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains only the full‑text paper and its corresponding data. The research focuses on resistance evaluation of tomato cultivars from Heilongjiang Province against Meloidogyne incognita . This is a research‑type paper. In this study, 21 tomato cultivars were collected from local markets, with the laboratory‑preserved resistant cultivar VFNT serving as the control. Greenhouse potted assays with artificial quantitative inoculation (1 000 eggs of Meloidogyne incognita per plant, inoculation duration of 42 days) were adopted to identify the resistance of each cultivar to southern root‑knot nematode ( Meloidogyne incognita ). Phenotypic responses after inoculation with northern root‑knot nematode ( M. hapla ) were used to verify whether candidate resistant cultivars carried the Mi‑1 gene. The measured indicators included root‑knot index, root fresh weight, number of egg masses per gram of root, and egg reproduction factor. Resistance grades including immune, highly resistant, resistant, moderately resistant, susceptible and highly susceptible were determined according to resistance‑grading criteria based on three indicators: root‑knot index, egg‑mass quantity and egg reproduction factor. The dataset consists of text and spreadsheet‑table files in pdf and xlsx formats, with a total data size of 1.13 MB. The main results are presented in Table 1, Table 2 and Table 3. Table 1 lists the origins of 21 tomato cultivars and the control; Table 2 shows the resistance evaluation of each cultivar against Meloidogyne incognita ; Table 3 presents the resistance evaluation of candidate cultivars against M. hapla . This dataset covers the research field of resistance identification for tomato cultivars in Heilongjiang Province, involving more than 20 major commercially‑available local cultivars.

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the paper “Quantifying the Energy Cost of Security in 5G Centralized Units” by Sofia Martins, Ana Aguiar and Peter Steenkiste, published at IEEE GreenCom 2026. It contains CPU energy measurements and hardware performance counter (PMC) profiles from a virtualized 5G Centralized Unit, User Plane (CU-UP). The data were collected while the CU's PDCP layer processed uplink or downlink user-plane traffic under different ciphering and integrity-protection settings, traffic loads and packet sizes. The dataset has 1,394 experimental runs . In each run, the CU's energy use and hardware events were monitored for 60 s while a traffic generator sent UDP traffic in one direction. It can be used to study the energy cost of 5G Access Stratum security (SNOW 3G and AES), to find energy bottlenecks in CU software, and to train energy models based on hardware events. Testbed CU-UP host: OpenAirInterface (OAI), tag 2026.w14, running on an Intel Core i9-13900K (32 logical CPUs) with the Linux performance CPU governor. The OS is Ubuntu Server 24.04.2 LTS with the 6.8.1-1015-realtime kernel. Traffic generator host: a second machine emulates the DU, CU-CP and UPF and runs a custom UDP traffic generator. GTP-U traffic is exchanged over the F1-U and NG-U interfaces on a 2.5 Gbps Ethernet link. Algorithm implementations: SNOW 3G is OAI's software implementation, based on the 3GPP reference code. AES-based algorithms use OpenSSL 3.0.13 with Intel AES-NI acceleration. PDCP settings: Robust Header Compression (RoHC) is disabled, DRBs are in Unacknowledged Mode, and there is 1 UE. PDCP headers are 2 bytes with a 12-bit sequence number, and security follows MAC-then-encrypt. Energy measurement: RAPL package domain (cores, caches and memory controller), read with turbostat . Idle power is measured before the CU process starts. Power during the 60 s monitoring window is sampled at 1 Hz and integrated to give energy in joules.
evidence_items.title: Quantifying the Energy Cost of Security in 5G Centralized Units

evidence_items.summary: This study investigates the performance of five large language models (LLMs) in assessing the complexity of student-generated help-seeking questions in a Chinese engineering course. Using 200 authentic student questions and the ratings of two domain experts as a task-specific reference, we evaluated GPT-4o mini, Claude-3.7-sonnet, DeepSeek-v3, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and SparkDesk-v3.1 under a standardized prompt and a three-trial evaluation protocol. The results revealed three main findings. First, all models showed strong positive rank correlations with expert judgments, but agreement varied across complexity levels. Notably, exact-match agreement was relatively high for Level 4 and Level 5 questions (90% and 99%, respectively), whereas it was lower for the intermediate levels (64% for Level 2 and 69% for Level 3), indicating a non-monotonic relationship between question complexity and classification agreement. Second, Claude-3.7-sonnet achieved the highest descriptive agreement with the expert reference, with the highest exact-match rate (89.5%) and the lowest mean absolute error (0.11). Third, model agreement and repeated-trial stability did not coincide: Gemini-2.5-Flash achieved the highest stability (97.5%), followed by DeepSeek-v3 (92%), while Claude-3.7-sonnet achieved 86%. These findings extend existing comparative evidence by demonstrating that model performance in student question-complexity assessment depends on both the complexity level being classified and the evaluation dimension being considered. The results support the potential use of LLMs for preliminary educational assessment, while emphasizing the need for task-specific validation and human oversight.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating student question complexity with large language models

organizations: Assistant Professor at Patel Law College, Patel Group of Institutions, Bengaluru, Karnataka, India
evidence_items.summary: An agentic artificial intelligence may make plans and perform interrelated digital acts, including communications, identity assertions and payment directives, with little human involvement. Where agentic AI is employed to defraud a victim, Indian criminal law must find the human agent behind the scheme without treating the outputs of the AI as an indicator of any individual’s guilt. The paper evaluates how far the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), the Information Technology Act, 2000 (IT Act), and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) can address fraud enabled by agentic AI. It demonstrates that existing offences cover a deliberately orchestrated fraud carried out through agentic AI, but are not suitable for attributing responsibility automatically to the owner or any other individual merely because the harm was foreseeable. The proposed delegation-sensitive model of attribution asks whether the accused chose the purpose of the deception, supplied the system with the necessary capabilities, knew of the risks involved, controlled the process and, finally, adopted it with full knowledge. These factors do not replace the elements of the offence or the prosecution’s burden of proof; they only structure the evidentiary base. The article also suggests guidelines on preserving the necessary evidence, structuring charges, maintaining proper audit logs for important systems and avoiding vicarious criminal liability.
evidence_items.title: Delegated Deception: Human Criminal Liability for Agentic AI Enabled Fraud under Indian Law

organizations: College of Management and Computer Application MIT Art, Design and Technology University
evidence_items.summary: The financial services industry is undergoing a structural shift from single-turn, reactive AI assistants toward autonomous, goal-oriented multi-agent systems, commonly termed “Agentic AI” or autonomous financial co-pilots. Unlike earlier generative AI tools that merely produce text or recommendations for human review, agentic systems can plan multi-step workflows, invoke external tools and data sources, and execute transactions within defined boundaries of autonomy. This paper examines the strategic, financial, and risk implications of this shift across corporate finance, banking, and asset management, evaluating impact through the lens of unit economics, operational efficiency, and risk-adjusted return. Drawing on evidence from financial-technology and risk-management literature — including work on AI-driven sentiment forecasting (Dash & Mishra, 2024a, 2024b; Mishra & Dash, 2025), blockchain-based control layers (Mishra & Phansalkar, 2025; Phansalkar et al., 2023), and credit and market risk frameworks (Dr. Ujjwal Mishra, 2016; Deepak Ranjan Sahoo, 2017) — the paper argues that agentic AI compresses operational cost structures and cycle times while introducing new categories of operational and systemic risk that demand deterministic governance layers, capital allocation limits, and human-in-the-loop validation. Illustrative figures and comparative tables are used throughout to frame the magnitude and shape of this shift. The paper closes with strategic recommendations for CFOs, FinTech leaders, and regulators navigating this transition over the next three to five years.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI & Autonomous Financial Co-Pilots: Transforming Decision-Making, Unit Economics, and Operational Risk in the Financial Sector

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the research paper entitled "Token-Efficient Cross-Lingual Generation: A Novel Generation-Language Selection Framework for Reducing Large Language Model Token Consumption" by Jincheng Zhang (Independent Researcher). The dataset supports the investigation of Token-Efficient Cross-Lingual Generation (TECLG), a framework that separates the language used for primary large language model (LLM) generation from the language required for final output delivery. The central research objective is to examine whether generating content in an alternative language before translating it into the requested target language can reduce primary-model generation-token consumption and generation time. Experimental Design The experiment involved 200 topics and two generation conditions: Group A – Direct Chinese Generation: The primary language model directly generated the requested content in Chinese. Group B – Cross-Lingual Generation: The primary language model generated content in English, which was subsequently translated into Chinese using a neural machine translation model. The experimental system employed Qwen3-8B (Q4 K M quantization), accessed through a local llama.cpp-compatible inference service, as the primary language model. Helsinki-NLP/OPUS-MT (English-to-Chinese) was used as the translation component. A total of 400 experimental records were expected. Of these, 396 were successfully completed, comprising 197 successful records in Group A and 199 in Group B. After matching observations by topic, 196 complete paired comparisons were available for statistical analysis. Dataset Contents and Evaluation Metrics The dataset is intended to document the experimental observations and quantitative results supporting the study. Relevant data categories include: Experimental topic identifiers and paired observations. Final Chinese output character counts. Final Chinese output token counts according to the Qwen tokenizer.
evidence_items.title: Dataset for Token-Efficient Cross-Lingual Generation (TECLG): Experimental Data and Evaluation Results

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains the Bombyx mori BmN4 pangenome graphs for 29 chromosomes. For each community, a pangenome graph was constructed using pggb (-s 5000 -l 25000 -p 90 -c 1 -K 19 -F 0.001 -g 30 -k 23 -f 0 -B 10M -n 1 -j 0 -e 0 -G 700,1100 -P 1,4,6,2,26,1 -O 0.001 -d 100 -Q Consensus ), with the BmN4 consensus genome as the reference and the Hifiasm.Hybrid primary and secondary contigs as input. The sequences were partitioned into 29 chromosome-corresponding communities, and a separate pangenome graph was generated for each community. The dataset includes: GFA files of the pangenome graphs for each chromosome - One GFA file per chromosome-based community - File naming convention: BmN4 chr[ID].gfa (e.g., BmN4 chr1.gfa , BmN4 chr2.gfa , ..., BmN4 chrW.gfa ) These resources provide a high-resolution view of structural variation and genome graph topology for the BmN4 genome, and can be used for further comparative genomics and pangenome visualization.

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used by the public to access health‐related information. However, most current evaluations are cross‐sectional studies, which may not capture changes resulting from model updates.Thunderstorm asthma presents an extremely challenging test scenario for the iterative evaluation of models. This study aims to conduct a longitudinal benchmark study comparing information on thunderstorm asthma generated by four widely available large language model (LLM) families ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Perplexity AI and Microsoft Copilot in terms of quality, safety, empathy, transparency and readability. Using the same 24 public‐facing queries based on Google Trends, three clinicians independently assessed safety, accuracy, empathy, discriminative power, EQIP, the JAMA benchmark criteria and GQS, yielding a total of 192 responses. Readability is measured using six established assessment criteria. Matching factors in the query structure were controlled for using cross‐sectional and matched longitudinal analyses. Multiple comparisons were performed using the Benjamini–Hochberg correction, supplemented by a mixed‐effects model. The results showed that inter‐rater reliability was consistently high. Between T1 and T2, the EQIP scores for all four model series improved significantly (all adjusted P < 0.001), with Perplexity AI (+22.43 points) and ChatGPT (+21.74 points) showing the greatest improvements. DISCERN improved significantly for ChatGPT (+6.58; adjusted P < 0.001) and Perplexity AI (+8.32; adjusted P < 0.001). However, after adjustment, none of the models exhibited a significant trend of longitudinal improvement in either the accuracy or GQS metrics. Safety metrics remained relatively stable, at time point T2, the safety response rate ranged from 79.2 per cent to 91.7 per cent, and no significant improvement was observed within each model family. Readability trajectories diverged markedly.
evidence_items.title: A Longitudinal Benchmark of Information Output From Large Language Models on Thunderclap Asthma: Quality, Safety, Empathy, and Readability

evidence_items.summary: Pretrained (foundation) time-series models are promoted as ready-to-use forecasters, but they have rarely been tested on African disease surveillance data, which are sparse, irregular and often revised. A second problem is that public series may already sit inside the data these models were trained on, which would make them look better than they are. This protocol fixes, in advance, a benchmark that compares pretrained models used without any tuning against simple statistical methods on 274 eligible surveillance series from across Africa (cholera, Lassa fever, measles, meningitis and mpox). The main test uses only observations dated after the models were released, so the models cannot have seen them. Data sources, eligibility rules, models, forecast horizons, scores, statistical tests and sensitivity analyses are all stated here before any forecast is run. Background and rationale Outbreak forecasting supports decisions on vaccines, staff and supplies. Health agencies in Africa usually have short, noisy count series and little computing capacity, so a model that works without local training would be valuable. Published evaluations of pretrained forecasting models rely mostly on energy, retail, traffic and high-income health data. Whether their performance carries over to African surveillance counts is not known. Because these models are trained on very large public collections, a fair test also needs data that did not exist when the models were built. Objectives 1. Primary: to test whether pretrained time-series models, used zero-shot, give more accurate probabilistic forecasts than a seasonal naive method on African surveillance series observed after the models' release. 2. Secondary: to compare them with standard statistical and machine-learning methods; to describe how performance changes with sparsity, disease, reporting frequency and series length; and to estimate how much apparent skill is lost between pre-release and post-release data.
evidence_items.title: Do pretrained time-series models forecast African disease surveillance data better than simple methods? Protocol for a pre-specified benchmark with a post-release hold-out v1
