evidence_items.summary: Accurate detection of small variants underpins population, functional and clinical genomics, yet short-read sequencing remains unreliable in repetitive and duplicated regions of the human genome, where long reads provide substantially greater sequence context. Although this disparity is well documented, aggregate accuracy metrics delineate where short- and long-read callsets diverge but not the mechanisms that give rise to these differences. Here, we present a region-stratified benchmark of single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) and insertion--deletion (INDEL) detection from Illumina short-read and PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing of the Genome in a Bottle reference sample HG002, evaluating multiple variant callers across genomic contexts, sequencing depths and INDEL lengths. Both platforms achieved near-complete accuracy in high-confidence regions, whereas short-read performance deteriorated in low-mappability regions and segmental duplications, a deficit that persisted with increasing sequencing depth. Within these regions, short-read recall declined toward the interiors of long tracts, with increasing sequence identity to the closest paralog and with greater distance from paralogous sequence variants, and these declines coincided with a pronounced excess of ambiguously placed reads. Together, these findings implicate ambiguous read placement as the predominant source of the short-read deficit, demonstrate that its magnitude can be anticipated from the length and paralog similarity of the surrounding sequence, and thereby delineate the genomic contexts in which long-read sequencing is most warranted.
evidence_items.title: A stratified benchmark reveals distinct short- and long-read performance gradients within difficult genomic regions

evidence_items.summary: Multi-agent debate and adversarial self-correction are frequently reported to improve or degrade factual accuracy, yet these pipelines end with an aggregation step whose contribution is rarely isolated. We show that this final step can dominate the reported effect. Holding adversarial transcripts fixed, we re-aggregate them on a 1,200-item Chinese factuality benchmark across three model families. On all 1,200 items, replacing the consensus-list aggregator with a minimal answer-first instruction raises accuracy from 58.8% to 76.7% (Δ = +17.9; up to +29.9 for one model). On a stratified 400-item subset, five aggregation strategies span 59.6%–86.2% (Δ = 26.5). The best strategy discards the debate transcript entirely and answers the question directly (86.2%), which is statistically indistinguishable from zero-shot answering (86.2–87.5%); every aggregator that consumes the adversarial transcript is worse (59.6%–77.6%). Pooled over models, the theory-prescribed consensus-list aggregator is the worst: it emits commentary rather than answers, and both automatic judging and human annotation become less reliable on its outputs (inter-annotator κ = 0.482; judge–human three-way agreement 56.7% and 55.0% for the two annotators). In our controlled setting, the aggregation stage alone can move accuracy by more than the effects attributed to debate in comparable studies; we therefore recommend that aggregation choices be reported and ablated before any claim about debate-based factuality is made.
evidence_items.title: Does Debate Help Factuality? A Controlled Re-Aggregation Study on a 1,200-Item Chinese Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Weather-path calibration can affect multi-day scheduling risk. We examine a semi-synthetic sea-to-shore benchmark using a three-state Markov chain fitted to 2024 NOAA wave observations, with January–September for fitting and October–December for holdout evaluation. The fitted chain has a holdout Frobenius error of 0.020 and Brier score of 0.111, while fit and holdout stationary distributions differ by 0.135 in total variation. Exact 240-h diagnostics show that calibration increases rough-state occupancy standard deviation from 0.052 to 0.173 and reduces expected state changes from 75.6 to 13.2. The reported scheduling benchmark mean increases from 42.36 to 53.31 h and CVaR0.95 from 50.57 to 112.61 h. These contrasts combine changes in transition dependence, state composition, and selected policies. A composition-controlled process diagnostic separates dependence from mean exposure before scheduling. With 18 equally weighted training scenarios, empirical CVaR0.95 equals the sample maximum. Observed-path comparisons, forecast baselines, specification tests, and pseudocount checks define the supported scope. Tests reject strict first-order dynamics and within-fit homogeneity; the chain serves as a working approximation. The study establishes input-law and tail-resolution sensitivity within this benchmark; operational prediction and unconditional completion-time tails require additional validation.
evidence_items.title: Stochastic-Process Calibration and Sensitivity Analysis for a Sea-to-Shore Scheduling Benchmark with Markovian Sea States

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT The transition of the photon from an effectively point‐like structure to hadron fluctuations at high energies requires a rigorous description of gluon dynamics in two‐photon collisions. To map this transition without resorting to purely empirical artifices, it becomes necessary to establish a controlled analytical baseline—a benchmark—that examines the foundations and operational limits of the color‐dipole framework. Because standard low‐energy frameworks like the Quark‐Parton Model and Vector Meson Dominance cannot accommodate the gluon component demanded by LEP results, we must evaluate the foundational limitations of the TKM and IKT prescriptions. We explicitly track their structural compromises—including exchange symmetry breaking, the homogeneous‐disk target approximation, and the hypothesis of universality—to understand where effective parameterizations substitute for first‐principles of QCD. By articulating the non‐linear Balitsky–Kovchegov evolution equation with five saturation models—GBW, IIMS, rcBK, AGBS, and WYKWC—the study maps the theoretical dispersion arising from different treatments of the saturation scale and coupling. This methodological reference aims to dimension systematic uncertainties, test the consistency of the dipole‐proton analogy, and subsidize data analysis in future electron–positron colliders, as treated in detail in the companion paper.
evidence_items.title: Two‐Photon Interactions at High Energies: Establishing a Theoretical Benchmark for the Color Dipole Formalism and Saturation Models

evidence_items.summary: This paper evaluates artificial intelligence (AI), Agentic AI, and autonomous AI as complete cybersecurity workflows. The paper makes three major contributions: (1) a hierarchical role-and-assurance taxonomy and cross-family synthesis that maps statistical analytics, deep learning, graph neural networks, large language models, and Agentic AI to distinct cybersecurity lifecycle roles; (2) an end-to-end, complete-workflow evaluation framework that integrates precision, recall, F1, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), latency, cost, drift, robustness, unsafe-action rates, escalation, rollback, and auditability; and (3) an empirical synthesis that identifies where modern AI delivers measurable gains over earlier analytics and defines the human-governed safeguards required for bounded, reversible autonomy. Accuracy alone can conceal delay, cost, tool misuse, policy violations, and irreversible actions. Evidence shows F1 = 97.36%, AUROC = 99.59%, and 0.0476 ms latency; drift adaptation increased F1 from 0.60 to 0.86; policy-bounded remediation reduced violations from 12.18% to 5.82%; and layered defenses left 8.4% residual indirect prompt-injection vulnerability. Modern AI performs best on heterogeneous, relational, and multi-step tasks; autonomy should expand only when incremental workflow benefit is measured and failures remain detectable, containable, attributable, and reversible. Keywords: cybersecurity, machine learning, graph neural networks, large language models, agentic AI
evidence_items.title: End-to-End Evaluation of AI, Agentic AI, and Autonomous Cybersecurity Systems

organizations: Department of Information Technology, University of the Cumberlands, Williamsburg, KY 40769, USA
evidence_items.summary: Safety checks on clinical large language model (LLM) agents usually inspect only their final output. We present a gateway that checks each action a clinical agent proposes before it runs, and allows it, defers it to a clinician or blocks it. It fuses five run-time signals (calibration among similar patients, subgroup calibration gaps, group-conditional conformal sets, drift state, alert timing) with a check that alerts quote tool outputs correctly. Agent trajectories were generated with a local 7-billion-parameter model on emergency department (ED) and intensive care (ICU) cohorts, six fault types designed around the signals were injected, and the configuration was frozen on a tuning split. In held-out ED trajectories this frozen gateway stopped 62% of the targeted faults at the fault step, against 31% for an output-only check, with false intervention on 7.0% of clean trajectories. On held-out ICU hospitals it deferred every request on its drift signal, so the ICU results support no deployment claim. Four faults not designed around any signal were stopped no more often than the same clean trajectories (ED difference +0.5 percentage points, 95% CI −1.3 to 2.1); detection was shown only for the targeted fault classes. On a Raspberry Pi 5, with the LLM on a workstation, the 99th-percentile latency per gated action was 25.8 ms. Post hoc per-site revisions remain unconfirmed.
evidence_items.title: A Step-Level Reliability Gateway for Agentic Clinical Decision Support: Architecture, Edge Deployment and Retrospective Evaluation on Targeted Fault Classes

evidence_items.summary: In the increasingly complex landscape of global supply chains, traditional procurement processes often struggle with data silos, manual inefficiencies, and delayed risk assessments. This paper proposes a novel framework for automating supplier selection via an agentic AI approach, focusing on a supplier scoring agent. Our approach decomposes the selection process into four specialized stages managed by agent entities: a requirement gathering agent, a supplier discovery agent, a supplier scoring agent, and a negotiation strategy agent. Additionally, within the risk-based evaluation phase, we introduce a unified NLP-Entropy-TOPSIS framework as the core underlying computational engine of the scoring agent. This agent continuously synthesizes disparate, unstructured data sources, such as global trade news and corporate sustainability reports, by filtering textual streams through Transformer architectures. The agent dynamically transitions the criteria states of the decision matrix using sentiment analysis. By automating the perception-reasoning loop, this modular architecture could reduce the cognitive load on procurement professionals while maintaining a critical human-in-the-loop component for final strategic oversight.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Adaptive Decision Matrix for Dynamic TOPSIS Green Supplier Selection

evidence_items.summary: Many customer-support teams now let a large language model draft email replies from a retrieval-augmented knowledge base. Such an agent can be misled by instructions that an attacker hides in the incoming email or plants in a knowledge-base document. In this paper we build a pinned benchmark for this setting and use it to measure how exposed an undefended pipeline really is. The benchmark has 1,800 cases: 1,000 attack emails written by participants of the LLMail-Inject challenge, 300 poisoned-document cases from PoisonedRAG, a seed knowledge base and synthetic templates, and 500 benign emails. The cases are drawn by seeded stratified sampling, fixed by a SHA-256 digest and replayed through a live host with triage, hybrid retrieval and one JSON reply call. Without any defense, 24.3% to 34.4% of the attack emails succeed end to end on GPT-4o-mini, Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B. Poisoned documents succeed in 22.7% of cases on GPT-4o-mini, but in 76.3% and 81.3% of cases on the two open models. A stricter prompt that tells the model where instructions may come from changes these rates by four points at most. We also find that two measurement choices matter a lot. Because triage closes many emails before any reply is written, end-to-end attack success can be only a third to a half of the rate among drafted replies, and a string-matching scorer counts up to twice as many successful email attacks as a meaning-based reading of the same drafts. Benchmarks of such pipelines should therefore report both.

evidence_items.summary: Synphly is a CASA pipeline for standard calibration, plotting and basic imaging of radio interferometric data from the VLA. It has been used to calibrate observations in all VLA bands, with bootstrapped flux densities within about 5% of the VLA pipeline on the test datasets. It runs on modular CASA ( casatools and casatasks ) in a standard Python environment, with one TOML configuration file per observation.

evidence_items.summary: Description This archive contains the derived data, gene set definitions, sample annotations, statistical outputs, and analysis code underlying the manuscript "Divergent autophagy programmes across cyst progression in polycystic kidney disease", submitted to the Journal of Nephrology. The study reanalysed five public, de-identified transcriptomic cohorts comprising 146 samples in total. No new human or animal samples were generated. Version 2.0.0 is a five-cohort extension and supersedes the earlier single-cohort v1 deposit. All primary data remain publicly available in the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus. The archive was prepared in line with the Oxford University Press Research Data Policy and the FAIR principles. Primary datasets GSE7869: human PKD1 cyst-size spectrum, Affymetrix GPL570 microarray, n = 21. GSE289843: human PKD1 individual cysts and microcystic tissue, bulk RNA sequencing, n = 55. GSE231304: mouse Pkd1 intra-kidney spatial progression, bulk RNA sequencing, n = 18. GSE220775: adult mouse Pkd1 knockout with or without salsalate, bulk RNA sequencing, n = 32. GSE261420: adult mouse Pkd2 knockout with quantitative kidney weight to body weight burden, bulk RNA sequencing, n = 20. Persistent links and primary citations for each series are recorded in metadata/cohorts manifest.csv . Contents of the archive metadata : cohort manifest, de-identified sample annotations for all five cohorts, definitions of ten autophagy modules and three cellular-composition signatures, and the exact MSigDB Hallmark and GO-BP gene sets used. derived data : per-sample module and pathway z-scores for each cohort, per-cohort statistical summaries, composition-adjusted OLS results, an 18-gene cross-cohort replication matrix, a unified five-cohort effect-size table, and sensitivity analyses including leave-one-out, normalisation, kidney-averaged, and sex-adjusted models.

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Each donated organ creates an urgent coordination challenge because clinical evidence, allocation priorities, and institutional approvals must be brought together quickly, securely, and transparently. Existing approaches support parts of this process, but ranking, information review, record protection, and workflow governance remain separate. This fragmentation obscures how evidence informs a recommendation and the authorized actions that follow. Methods We present an integrated blockchain and large language model (LLM) decision support system connecting transparent ranking, constrained note review, deterministic safeguards, encrypted records, and authorized workflow actions. Structured attributes establish organ-specific reference rankings. The LLM only assigns predefined readiness states from notes, receives no rank information, and cannot select recipients. The safeguard excludes candidates on temporary hold and preserves the order of those remaining, while smart contracts govern the workflow. We evaluated the system using a synthetic dataset informed by public organ allocation guidance and clinically relevant compatibility, urgency, logistics, and readiness factors. The dataset comprised 1,600 training, 320 validation, and 400 independent test cases balanced across kidney, liver, heart, and lung workflows. Results Fine-tuned Qwen and GPT-4o mini returned valid and complete outputs in 93.0% and 97.0% of cases, with macro F1 scores of 99.3% and 99.6% among valid and complete outputs, respectively. When every candidate in an unsuccessful case was counted as incorrectly classified, the corresponding overall macro F1 scores were 95.3% and 98.0%. The selected primary recipient agreed with the synthetic reference in 372 and 387 cases, respectively. In a post hoc robustness analysis, all 20 scenarios produced the expected selection or stopped safely without creating a decision.
evidence_items.title: An integrated blockchain and large language model decision support system for organ donation and transplantation workflows

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The VU Amsterdam Metaphor Corpus (VUAMC) underlies VUA-18/VUA-20, the most widely used metaphor-detection benchmark. We show that one of its 117 fragments – b1g, an academic text on geographic information systems – was annotated only in part: 3,006 lexical units according to the corpus creators’ Appendix A, whereas the distributed TEI XML contains the full 20,170-word section. Because the encoding cannot distinguish the absence of annotation from a negative judgment, the benchmark conversion turned some 17,148 unannotated lexical units into negative gold labels. In benchmark units, this is 9,287 target tokens, 12.8% of the VUA-18 all pos training set, carrying 3 positive labels, with a lemma prior predicting about 1,635 (z = − 53.66). Eight independent layers of evidence point to this one section, among them the creators’ documentation, a second annotation layer, the published academic metaphor rate, and the shared task’s own unexplained register anomaly. None of the eight relies on a model or on training. Once this supervision is removed, a bert-base token classifier rises from 0.7070 to 0.7200 F1 (+ 0.0131, 95% CI [+ 0.0082, + 0.0194]); removing an equal number of randomly selected tokens brings no such gain (− 0.0030). The Verbs track replicates the result (+ 0.0207), and cross-validation over the corpus finds gains in all four registers rather than in the academic one alone (+ 0.0081). The test set is left intact, so every published test result still stands. We release the corrected split and argue that wherever a format cannot tell absence from negativity, partial annotation can silently become supervision
evidence_items.title: Silent negatives: when partial annotation becomes supervision. A label integrity audit of the VU Amsterdam Metaphor Corpus benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Computer-using agents are increasingly expected to complete realistic user goals rather than isolated GUI actions. However, existing benchmarks typically isolate web, mobile, or desktop environments, leaving it unclear whether a single generalist agent can execute long-horizon workflows that span multiple operating systems and persistent application states. We introduce OS-Omni, a live cross-platform benchmark and execution environment for evaluating computer-using agents across Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, iOS, Android, and Web environments. OS-Omni is released in versioned waves of 300 tasks each; this paper focuses on the first release, v1, which contains 48 tasks per platform and 12 cross-platform workflows that pair a desktop with an Android phone. OS-Omni provides reproducible initialization, platform-specific adapters, trajectory logging, and executable final-state evaluators, and includes controlled service-backed applications for workflows involving account, cart, budget, calendar, message, and other persistent state. Human studies show that OS-Omni tasks require 67.54 interaction steps, substantially exceeding OSWorld references of 15.0 steps. On v1, the strongest evaluated agent, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches 68.5% average success, trailing the 77.3% human reference by 8.8 points; the gap is uneven across platforms, with frontier models exceeding humans on Linux but trailing them by more than 25 points on iOS and macOS. These results indicate that current agents remain far from platform-robust, long-horizon computer use, especially when success requires sustained state tracking and durable final-state changes.
evidence_items.title: OS-Omni: Benchmarking Generalist Computer-Using Agents on Long-Horizon Workflows Across Platforms

evidence_items.summary: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.
evidence_items.title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents

evidence_items.summary: Objectives Large language models are increasingly used in evidence synthesis, but high accuracy among returned values may coexist with consequential omissions. We evaluated a stateless, source-grounded artificial intelligence (AI) workflow for extracting data from primary randomized-trial reports and reconstructing meta-analyses. Methods The fixed corpus comprised 15 randomized trials from a published review of regional anesthesia for pediatric cardiac surgery. For each trial report, one stateless extraction attempt was made with GPT-5.6-sol through the application programming interface (API), using the primary-report PDF and a frozen prompt and schema. No review material was supplied at inference time. A transport-only retry was permitted only when no scientific output had been produced. The reference standard was a manually source-verified universe of target-positive cells. Outcomes included composite reconstruction accuracy, precision, completeness, source support, rescue performance, and pooled-estimate reconstruction. Results Thirteen primary calls produced contract-valid outputs; two completed outputs failed the support contract. Of 1,657 evaluable cells, 821 satisfied the preregistered composite requirement for exact content and adequate source support (49.55%). Among 897 positive claims, 892 were content-exact (99.44%), 823 had adequate support (91.75%), and 821 met both criteria (protocol-composite precision 91.53%). Completeness was 54.13%, and 760 source-present cells were omitted. Effect direction agreed in all 11 syntheses estimable from both input sets, but only eight used the same study set; four of 15 source-based syntheses were not estimable from AI inputs. Both failed trials produced a valid first rescue output, with 173 of 284 cells exact and supported (60.92%).

evidence_items.summary: The growing popularity of large language models (LLMs) over the last five years has produced a large amount of technical documentation and research that are published almost exclusively in English. For low-resource languages such as Bulgarian this creates a twofold gap: a lack of accessible, systematic descriptions of the LLMs in Bulgarian, and a lack of an agreed terminology for the fundamental technical concepts. These gaps impede AI literacy, regulatory compliance under EU AI-related legislation, and the understanding of AI concepts by the wider public. This paper presents an integrated resource that aims to take the first steps towards addressing these gaps for Bulgarian. The first component is a structured database of LLM descriptions (currently, 453 from 38 model families), covering open-weight, proprietary, and Bulgarian-, Slavic- and Balkan-oriented models. The description is organised in a Neo4j graph database with information on architecture, training data, training methods, benchmarks, licensing, access conditions. The second component is a bilingual English–Bulgarian terminology dictionary of LLM-related concepts (currently comprising 358 entries, of which 305 are verified—111 attested in Bulgarian sources and 194 newly proposed) across nine thematic domains. The two components are linked: the terms for architectures, training methods and applications used in the descriptions are taken from the dictionary, so that a revision of a term is propagated to all descriptions that use it. The resources are released under the CC-BY-4.0 licence with a web interface in Bulgarian for search and filtering of LLMs. The intended use of the resources is to support research, education, and public engagement with AI in Bulgaria.
evidence_items.title: System for Describing Large Language Models in Bulgarian

evidence_items.summary: Abstract DNA repair pathways safeguard genome integrity yet are frequently dysregulated in cancer and other human diseases. In tumors, DNA repair defects drive tumor evolution while creating therapeutic vulnerabilities exploitable by chemotherapy, DNA damage-response inhibitors, and immunotherapy. Although pathway-focused studies have elucidated key repair mechanisms, they lack the scale needed to interpret the high-dimensional genomic, transcriptomic, imaging, structural, and clinical datasets generated by modern precision oncology. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning help address this gap by offering new ways to measure DNA repair activity, predict repair outcomes, and connect diverse biological data. Here we organize AI applications in DNA repair into a biology-driven three-wave framework: mutational footprint-based repair-state inference; lesion-level repair outcome prediction; and multimodal repair-state inference for biomarker discovery, therapy response prediction, synthetic lethality, and structure-guided drug discovery. We go beyond cataloging AI applications by evaluating their strengths, limitations, and appropriate use. We also clarify how AI findings should be interpreted from predictive correlations to experimentally supported mechanisms. Finally, we discuss challenges in model transparency, dataset bias, imperfect labels, overfitting, validation, and clinical translation, and outline principles for developing biologically grounded AI frameworks that advance mechanistic discovery and precision oncology.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in DNA repair: from mechanism to medicine

evidence_items.summary: Wheat production requires approaches linking genetic improvement with mechanical harvesting. However, research on wheat genetics, digital phenotyping, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled harvesting remains fragmented. This review links genetic markers, harvest-related traits, digital sensing, and AI for smart wheat harvesting. Harvestability is defined as the capacity of a wheat crop to make its grain recoverable by harvesting machinery under defined field and operating conditions, evaluated through grain recovery and harvest losses. It assesses markers associated with yield components, lodging, maturity, and threshability, and sensing and AI methods for crop characterization, yield prediction, and harvest-loss monitoring. It distinguishes biological-yield prediction from mechanical harvest-loss estimation and considers model validation and transferability. Evidence indicates that digital phenotyping and yield prediction are more established than integrated approaches to predicting or reducing combine-harvester losses. Barriers include scarce datasets integrating genetic, phenotypic, environmental, and machine-operation data, inconsistent loss-measurement protocols, and limited independent field validation. A six-stage framework is proposed, linking genetic potential and crop traits to environmental conditions, sensing, AI-based prediction, harvesting decisions, and measured outcomes. The novelty lies in connecting wheat genetics and harvestability with AI-enabled harvesting decisions while distinguishing established applications from proposed integration pathways requiring field validation to demonstrate loss reduction.
evidence_items.title: Wheat Harvestability: Genetic Markers and Artificial Intelligence for Smart Harvesting

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Sample planarity is rarely monitored in fluorescence microscopy quality control. Here we describe FlatStat, a tool that estimates sample tilt automatically from any 3D fluorescence stack, and applied it to 1187 images from 20 public datasets. This revealed that tilt is ubiquitous across laboratories (median: 1.28 μm/100 μm), strongly structured across projects, and associated with a modest but detectable increase in chromatic shift (~57 nm). FlatStat is freely available as an ImageJ macro and Python script (doi: 10.5281/zenodo.20325392 ).
evidence_items.title: From User Complaint to Community Benchmark: Leveraging the Image Data Resource for Sample Planarity Quality Control

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate full-energy peak efficiency (FEPE) calibration of high-purity germanium (HPGe) detectors is essential for quantitative gamma-ray spectrometry and numerous applications in nuclear science and technology. Although Monte Carlo radiation-transport simulations and efficiency-transfer techniques are widely employed for detector efficiency determination, their implementation often requires detailed detector characterization and considerable computational effort. In the present study, the Direct Mathematical Method (DMM) was evaluated as an analytical alternative through comparison with experimental measurements, EFFTRAN calculations, and Geant4-based RayXpert simulations reported for a 78.5% relative-efficiency n-type coaxial HPGe detector. The detector-response parameter required by the DMM, namely the effective photopeak attenuation coefficient, was derived from the experimental efficiency data and subsequently used to predict FEPE values over a wide gamma-ray energy range. Calculated efficiencies were compared with experimental, EFFTRAN, and RayXpert results using relative-deviation analysis together with statistical performance indicators, including the coefficient of determination (R²), root-mean-square error (RMSE), and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE). The DMM accurately reproduced the experimental efficiency curve across the investigated energy range, yielding absolute relative deviations ranging from 0.09% to 0.92%, with a mean absolute deviation of only 0.38%. These results demonstrate substantially better agreement with the experimental data than both RayXpert and EFFTRAN.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark Validation of the Direct Mathematical Method for HPGe Detector Efficiency Calibration Against Experimental Data, EFFTRAN, and Geant4-Based RayXpert Simulations

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Modern deepfake methods can create fake faces that are very difficult to detect just by watching a video. Therefore, practical deepfake-detection systems must be accurate while using limited computing resources. CNN-based methods analyse individual frames and can identify visual signs of manipulation, but they may miss unnatural changes between consecutive frames. Video Transformers can analyse these changes over time, but they usually require substantial computational power. A more practical approach is to combine CNNs for analysing facial details with recurrent and attention-based models for studying changes across frames. However, only a limited number of studies have tested such combined methods on realistic videos containing multiple people, where some faces may be manipulated while others remain genuine. This paper describes and evaluates an integrated architecture for video-level deepfake classification. Spatial features are extracted by an EfficientNet-B0 backbone augmented with a multi-scale, attention-refined feature path; the resulting 1,280-dimensional frame embeddings are processed by a two-layer bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) network with an additive temporal attention mechanism that rescales each frame representation by a learned weight; and the weighted sequence is refined by a single-layer Transformer encoder with four attention heads before temporal averaging and binary classification. Training employs gradient accumulation, mixed-precision arithmetic, chunked frame processing, exponential moving averaging of parameters and differential learning rates, enabling 45-frame sequences to be trained on a single 12 GB consumer graphics processing unit. The architecture was evaluated on a subset of the FFIW-10K benchmark using a held-out evaluation set of 1,987 instances, comprising 998 real (50.23%) and 989 fake (49.77%).
evidence_items.title: An Integrated Spatio-Temporal Architecture for Deepfake Video Classification: An Evaluation on the FFIW-10K Multi-Person Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) connected biomedical devices, wearable sensing, medical imaging analytics, electronic health record (EHR) intelligence, genomics, smart home monitoring, and telehealth platforms have opened new possibilities for proactive detection. Yet their impact remains constrained by fragmented implementation, limited interoperability, insufficient clinical integration, and unresolved governance challenges. This paper develops global agentic healthcare intelligence (GAHI) as a sociotechnical framework for integrating AI-enabled healthcare intelligence technologies in ageing systems. It introduces the sociotechnical health intelligence transformation model (SHITM), which explains transformation as the alignment of technological intelligence, healthcare value creation, and societal legitimacy. Using comparative framework synthesis and integrative literature review methods, the article evaluates 30 healthcare intelligence technologies based on clinical relevance, early detection capability, AI maturity, scalability, governance risk, ageing applicability, and implementation readiness. The analysis proposes an early detection capability index (EDCI) and a governance risk score (GRS) to support structured evaluation. GAHI is then articulated as a six-layer architecture comprising data acquisition, intelligence processing, agentic decision systems, clinical intelligence, governance and compliance, and population health intelligence (HI). The framework advances biomedical engineering, health informatics, AI governance, gerontechnology, and sustainable health-system design by moving from isolated digital applications toward interoperable, explainable, privacy-preserving, and clinically actionable intelligence ecosystems.
evidence_items.title: Global Agentic Healthcare Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning intrusion and breach detectors are often reported at near-ceiling accuracy, yet a score supports a deployment decision only if its evaluation measures the intended generalisation. We integrate seven companion audits, covering eleven public collections from nine source captures in four data modalities, and derive the conditions an evaluation must meet for its score to be interpretable. Four domains recurred: protocol (does the split test the stated target?), acquisition (are labels separable from capture conditions?), operational (does performance hold at a stated false-alarm budget and prevalence?) and label (do labels reflect the mechanism or the annotator?). In a structural causal model, acquisition–label aliasing makes deployment performance non-identifiable, and only annihilating aggregators respect this non-compensatory structure. No collection passed all four domains; protocol effects depended on task rather than model; and precursor-stage attacks, the early-warning target for ransomware, were detected at about half the rate of impact-stage attacks at 1% false-alarm rate. We provide a 28-item audit instrument with a seven-item minimum viable audit and falsification criteria. The framework is derived, not yet validated.
evidence_items.title: Measuring What Matters: Capture-Aware Evaluation Validity in Machine-Learning Intrusion and Breach Detection, Necessary Conditions Derived from Seven Benchmark Audits

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We develop the concept of bounded delegated agency to explain how AI shopping services reduce consumer effort while preserving decision authority. Drawing on delegation, self-determination and service-value perspectives, we analyse two respondent-level datasets (N = 1,920) using factorial regression models with HC3 robust standard errors and bootstrap-based indirect association analysis. Results indicate that greater AI autonomy increases perceived task offloading, while reversibility reduces perceived agency encroachment and strengthens continued delegation intention, without demonstrated improvements in preference congruence or recommendation discrimination. Under high autonomy and low reversibility, consumer-priority disclosure is associated with an 8.91-percentage-point increase in recommendation acceptance compared with commercial-objective disclosure. Measurement summaries satisfy conventional reliability and validity thresholds. However, unavailable execution logs constrain causal interpretation and verification of actual restoration. The findings distinguish psychological reassurance from effective consumer protection, extending AI service research by demonstrating that greater acceptance and perceived control do not necessarily translate into better decision outcomes. Practically, AI service providers should establish explicit execution permissions, reliable reversal mechanisms and transparent objectives while evaluating both consumer perceptions and actual decision protection.
evidence_items.title: Governing agentic AI in marketing: Bounded delegated agency and consumer decision authority in shopping services

evidence_items.summary: Background: Neck of femur fractures impose a significant burden on elderly patients, demanding anaesthetic regimens that combine rapid onset with prolonged analgesia and haemodynamic stability. Isobaric ropivacaine 0.75%, though safer than bupivacaine, has limited duration when used alone. Aim:   This study evaluated the effect of 5 µg dexmedetomidine as an intrathecal adjuvant to isobaric ropivacaine 0.75% on spinal block characteristics in patients undergoing neck of femur fracture surgery. Methods: A prospective observational study was conducted at the Department of Anaesthesiology and Critical Care, Government Medical College, Srinagar, over 18 months (July 2024 – January 2026) enrolling 50 adult patients (ASA I–II) undergoing elective or urgent orthopaedic surgery for femoral neck fracture. All patients received an intrathecal injection of isobaric ropivacaine 0.75% (22.5 mg/3 mL) combined with dexmedetomidine 5 µg (0.5 mL). Sensory block onset, motor block characteristics, haemodynamic parameters, postoperative VAS scores, and complications were systematically recorded. Results: Mean sensory onset was 6.82 ± 0.75 min and motor onset was 7.56 ± 1.20 min. Maximum sensory and motor heights were achieved at 11.02 ± 0.80 and 12.34 ± 0.75 min, respectively. The mean duration of sensory blockade was 417.04 ± 7.19 min, motor blockade 392.04 ± 5.55 min, and complete analgesia 419.70 ± 4.78 min. VAS scores remained 0.00 for the first 6 hours postoperatively. Haemodynamic changes were statistically significant (p < 0.001) but remained within 20% of baseline. Zero complications (hypotension, bradycardia, nausea, vomiting, shivering, or respiratory depression) were recorded.
evidence_items.title: Dexmedetomidine 5 µg as an Adjuvant to Isobaric Ropivacaine 0.75% in Spinal Anaesthesia for Neck of Femur Fracture Surgery: Evaluation of Block Characteristics and Haemodynamic Safety:  A Prospective Observational Study

evidence_items.summary: Nature Quotient (NQ) describes the capacity to perceive and process information about how humans and nature interact. It has so far lacked a mechanism inside a formal theory of how minds take in information. This paper supplies one, using Mindsponge theory (MT). In MT, how much a mind examines incoming information depends on trust and on the energy cost of examining it. We propose that NQ lowers that cost for information about nature, and only for that information. Three propositions follow. NQ raises the weight a person gives to evidence about nature; it leaves the weight of evidence in other domains unchanged; and, in MT’s canonical form, it scales the whole profile of evidence weight across trust by a constant factor. We test these predictions on the International Social Survey Programme 2020 (28 countries, about 38,000 respondents), with time spent in nature as the NQ proxy. Each rule was fixed, simulated on the real data structure and fingerprinted before outcomes were opened. People who often spend time in nature gave their own experience of extreme weather roughly 1.7 to 2 times the weight that others gave it (+0.14 to +0.19 logit per standard deviation; z from 3.5 to 4.1 in three model specifications on the same data; implied multiplier 2.0, standard error 0.4). The same people gave no extra weight to evidence outside nature, their own low social position, when judging income redistribution (difference z = 2.11). The predicted concentration of the gain among people neutral toward the source was not found. MT–NQ thus gives NQ a precise role: it lowers the cost of evaluating nature evidence, so that evidence counts for more. The role is specific to nature and distinct from general engagement.
evidence_items.title: Nature Quotient Lowers the Cost of Evaluating Nature Information: A Mindsponge Model with Tests in 28 Countries

evidence_items.summary: Scarcity of groundwater and concerns about the quality of water has become a major challenge in Otukpo, a town located in southern Benue Trough in Nigeria. This study integrates Ground-Penetrating Radar (GPR), Electrical Resistivity Tomography (ERT) and Vertical Electrical Sounding (VES) with hydrogeochemical assessment to characterize subsurface formations, identify potential groundwater-bearing zones and evaluate the water-quality characteristics and possible contamination concerns of selected water sources in Otukpo. The VES interpretation indicated a four-layer geoelectric succession, with candidate groundwater-bearing intervals occurring at approximate depths of 28–72 m, interpreted resistivity values of 60–400 Ωm and estimated thicknesses of 32–37 m. ERT sections revealed relatively conductive anomalies of approximately 10–60 Ωm within an estimated depth interval of 30–45 m, which may be associated with weathered, fractured, clay-rich or water-saturated formations. These anomalies were treated as potential groundwater exploration targets rather than confirmed aquifers. The GPR results revealed shallow subsurface reflection patterns and possible discontinuities within an estimated effective investigation depth of approximately 4–15 m. Late-time reflections were interpreted cautiously in the two-way travel-time domain and were not treated as direct confirmation of deeper groundwater-bearing formations. Hydrogeochemical evaluation encompasses 40 designated samples consisting of 10 surface water, 10 newly dug well and 20 already existing well water samples. The analyses carried out on these samples include turbidity, pH, total dissolved solids, electrical conductivity and specific high-density metals, consisting copper (Cu), lead (Pb), manganese (Mn) and cadmium (Cd).
evidence_items.title: Integrated Geophysical Investigation for Sustainable Groundwater Development and Public Health Improvement in Otukpo Community

evidence_items.summary: Single-particle cryoEM is increasingly applied to compositionally complex, coarsely purified samples, whose micrographs often contain contaminants, including crystalline ice, aggregates, grid support material, and residual ethane. This contamination is spatially localized, occupying only part of an otherwise usable image such that rejecting whole micrographs would discard usable particles along with the contaminant. As data collection and processing grow more automated with less manual curation, this contamination becomes a greater liability, with contaminant-associated picks entering the particle stack and negatively impacting 3D refinement. These observations have motivated the development of tools to exclude contaminated regions of the image from analysis. Here we present cryoFILTER (Fourier-Informed Learning with Transformers for Excluding contaminated Regions), a framework for spatially selective micrograph curation that combines information from real-space images with local Fourier-space features and broader spatial context. Across held-out datasets, we find that these representations are highly complementary, distinguishing contamination from particle-bearing ice more accurately than isolated real-space or Fourier-space representations alone. Applying cryoFILTER to representative datasets removes contaminant-associated picks that classification does not reliably reject, while preserving nearby usable particles. This filtering yields more isotropic and interpretable reconstructions, more reproducible 2D classification, and, in an E. coli lysate, improved recovery of distinct ribosomal states. We additionally developed a lightweight classifier that assigns each detected contaminant region to its likely physical source, which we envision will aid in assessing the relative merits of different grid preparation and data collection approaches.
evidence_items.title: Localizing and labeling contamination in electron micrographs with cryoFILTER

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) acquire their capabilities primarily through scaling, and the rapidly rising cost of training has turned compute-budget allocation into a central practical concern. Classical scaling laws express loss as a function of model size and data volume only, and therefore cannot quantify data quality or domain mixture, two factors that are increasingly decisive in modern pre-training. This paper develops a three-stage framework for a generalized scaling law. First, the classical power law is fitted to 1,176 standardized Pythia training points by multi-start nonlinear least squares, with row- and block-bootstrap confidence intervals. Second, four quality-augmented candidate forms are compared on a held-out N-D-Q experiment grid; the additive form, in which the quality penalty enters linearly with the quality deficit, is selected, and a large supplementary matrix is identified as contaminated by its reversed quality monotonicity, its violations of the entropy floor, and the sign reversal of its quality coefficient when pooled. Third, the law is unified with centered-log-ratio domain-mixture coordinates, from which equal-loss substitution rates, elasticities, and compute-normalized marginal gains are derived analytically. The classical law attains an RMSE of 0.00011 nat with stable exponents across five data sources; the quality law reaches a hold-out correlation of 0.99; and the predictions remain accurate for models up to ten trillion parameters, where quality improvement proves up to 30,000 times more cost-effective than parameter scaling. The framework thus provides a quantitative basis for compute-constrained resource allocation in LLM pre-training.
evidence_items.title: A THREE-STAGE GENERALIZED SCALING LAW FOR LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL PRE-TRAINING

evidence_items.summary: Extreme rainfall and rapid urbanization have significantly increased the strain on urban drainage systems, leading to frequent sewer overflow events that pose serious risks to public health, infrastructure, and environmental sustainability. Traditional prevention strategies rely on passive mechanisms that are highly susceptible to dynamic uncertainties, such as sensor noise and inaccurate rainfall predictions, limiting their reliability in real-world deployment. To address these challenges, we propose MoE-SOP , a Multimodal M ixture of E xperts S ewer O verflow P revention Framework, which integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) with a multimodal expert reasoning architecture. MoE-SOP introduces a multimodal perception layer, where specialized expert models process diverse data sources to achieve robust system awareness: (1) the Information Expert leverages LLMs to analyze structured text data, extract critical insights, and generate decision support; (2) the Structural Expert employs a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) to model the spatial topology of the drainage system and enhance resilience against uncertainty through masked training; (3) the Image Expert processes simulator-rendered visual data to detect overflow anomalies. To ensure optimal decision-making, MoE-SOP incorporates a gated expert decision layer, which adaptively fuses insights via an attention-driven mechanism to generate proactive, context-aware control actions. To evaluate its effectiveness, MoE-SOP is tested within a Stormwater Management Model (SWMM) simulation environment under extreme rainfall conditions and high sensor noise. Experimental results show that MoE-SOP reduces overflow volume by 27.3% and maintains 89.7% overflow prevention performance under 20% sensor noise, significantly outperforming reinforcement learning and model predictive control baselines. Our findings highlight the potential of multimodal expert-guided frameworks in enhancing real-time, adaptive urban flood management.
evidence_items.title: MoE-SOP: Sewer Overflow Prevention via Multimodal Mixture of Experts Large Language Model

evidence_items.summary: A reasoning prompt can state a number without stating what the number is: "the lift carries 34 people" gives a capacity or a head count. We call this the role of a value: what the value stands for in the world the prompt describes. We introduce STAR-Clarify, a benchmark of 396 prompts generated from declared worlds. The expected behavior of each prompt (answer, ask, or report an impossibility) is set by its construction, and the answer under each reading is computed. About half of the prompts are clear, so that asking about everything is penalized. We also describe a short skill, built on the categories Things, States, Actions and Relationships (STAR), that asks a model to declare the world of a prompt before reasoning. On the ambiguous prompts, Claude Opus 5.5 resolves 20% silently and Qwen3-30B-A3B 65%. With the skill these shares fall to 0% and 13%. A control prompt that only tells the model to state its reading, without STAR, removes most of the silent resolutions on one-step prompts (24% remain). The skill keeps its advantage where the role of a value is open, including on verbs it never names. Inside a planning problem it removes an error on clear wording, in which the model plans with a stated capacity as if it were an amount (23 of 30 prompts without the skill, 0 with it). Asked to judge the wording, the smaller model calls 80% of the prompts it resolved silently unclear: it notices most of these problems and does not report them when it solves.
evidence_items.title: STAR-Clarify: A Role-Ambiguity Benchmark and a Clarification Skill for Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Rolling bearings are critical components in industrial rotating machinery, and their failures may cause unexpected downtime, economic loss, and safety risks. Although deep learning and multimodal fusion have improved vibration-based fault diagnosis, two issues remain insufficiently addressed: magnitude-dominated time–frequency representations may discard phase-related impulse timing information, and heterogeneous diagnostic cues are often fused without explicit alignment in a semantically consistent representation space. This paper proposes M2-LLM-FD, a lightweight large language model-assisted framework for semantic-aware multimodal evidence integration in rolling bearing fault diagnosis. The framework converts each vibration segment into three complementary forms: time-domain patch tokens, phase-aware time–frequency tokens, and structured statistical prompts. A phase-preserving complex convolutional dimensionality reduction network is designed to process the real and imaginary components of the time–frequency representations, thereby retaining phase-sensitive information associated with fault-induced impulsive events. A structured multimodal alignment and fusion module then harmonizes temporal granularity and projects the aligned evidence into the pretrained language-model embedding space through semantic-anchor cross-modal attention. Furthermore, domain-specific prior knowledge is injected via structured statistical prompts, and the model is efficiently fine-tuned using Low-Rank Adaptation. Extensive experiments on the CWRU, PU, and HUST datasets show that the proposed framework achieves consistent improvements in diagnostic accuracy, robustness, and cross-dataset generalization. Ablation and controlled analyses further validate the contributions of phase-aware time–frequency modeling, structured statistical prompts, and semantic-aware multimodal alignment to the overall diagnostic performance.
evidence_items.title: Semantic-aware multimodal evidence integration with a lightweight large language model for rolling bearing fault diagnosis

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Leaf functional traits are crucial for understanding plant ecology and ecosystem function. Specific leaf area (SLA)—the ratio of leaf area to dry mass—reflects plant resource acquisition strategies. However, global medium-resolution (30 m) SLA maps remain scarce due to sparse site observations and spatial scale mismatches. Here, we present a modular framework combining large language models (LLMs), machine learning, Landsat optical observations, and environmental variables to generate the first global 30 m SLA dataset with uncertainty estimates. First, LLMs completed missing plant functional type traits in the TRY database (growth form, leaf type, and phenology) with high accuracies (94.70–99.70%), maximizing data utility. Second, a novel landcover-based matching approach aligned site observations with 30 m spatial predictors, overcoming coordinate imprecision. Finally, a Random Forest model on Google Earth Engine integrated spectral, climatic, topographic, and soil layers to map SLA globally. This continuous 30 m SLA dataset addresses key spatial limitations of site observations, while the extensible processing chain can be adapted to other functional traits to support global ecosystem modeling.
evidence_items.title: Global 30 m Specific Leaf Area Dataset Integrating Large Language Model Imputation and Satellite Remote Sensing

evidence_items.summary: Background: Fungi are important pathogens and biotechnology resources, but lack a broadly applicable fungal DNA language model. Models trained on diverse fungal genomes can support functional interpretation of genomic variants and a broad range of genomic tasks. Results: We introduce FunDLM, a family of four DNA language models pre-trained on 426 fungal reference assemblies spanning 217 genera and 14.3 Gb of sequence. Without task-specific training, FunDLM-Medium-1024bp distinguished phenotype-associated missense variants of Saccharomyces cerevisiae from synonymous controls with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.875. It performed comparably to Evo 2, a generalist model with about 15 times more parameters, and better than Nucleotide Transformer v3. The model also recognized mutations that disrupt start codons or introduce premature stop codons in S. cerevisiae and the blast fungus Pyricularia oryzae. Its scores for missense variants, computed from DNA alone, correlated with those of protein language models in S. cerevisiae and two Fusarium species (Pearson correlation 0.57-0.75). After fine-tuning, FunDLM-Small-1024bp identified supernumerary chromosome sequences in four Pyricularia isolates not used for training (average precision 0.884), and FunDLM-Medium-1024bp recognized centromeres on a chromosome withheld from training (AUROC 0.908). Fine-tuned models also predicted three histone modifications in an isolate and on chromosomes not used for training (AUROC 0.910-0.996). Conclusions: FunDLM provides reusable sequence representations for assessing functional impacts of fungal variants as well as annotation of genomic and epigenomic features. The released models, data, code, and benchmarks support applications across fungal species.
evidence_items.title: FunDLM: A Foundation DNA Language Model for Fungi

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable fluency in natural language generation, yet they continue to struggle with structured reasoning tasks, including formal deduction, abstraction, multi-step inference, and prompt sensitivity. These limitations pose significant barriers to their deployment in high-stakes domains such as law, science, and healthcare. To address these deficiencies, this survey presents a comprehensive taxonomy of LLM reasoning deficiencies, illustrated with empirical case studies. We further examine four complementary enhancement paradigms—Chain-of-Thought prompting, training data optimization, program-aided reasoning, and mathematical model-aided inference—each targeting distinct reasoning challenges. To unify these approaches, we introduce the Adaptive Hybrid Reasoning Framework (AHRF), a modular, task-aware architecture that integrates symbolic logic, neuro-symbolic inference, program-level verification, reinforcement learning, and feedback-driven optimization. AHRF dynamically orchestrates reasoning strategies based on task structure and supports verifiable, semantically grounded inference. Guided by this framework, we identify six open challenges—scalability, interpretability, integration robustness, data dependency, ethical governance, and multimodal support—and propose corresponding research directions. This work offers a unified roadmap for advancing robust, explainable, and trustworthy reasoning in LLMs.
evidence_items.title: Advancing Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models: Issues, Challenges, and Pathways Forward

evidence_items.summary: Fire and gas leakage incidents remain a leading cause of preventable casualties and property loss, yet most conventional detection systems lack real-time remote notification, multi-modal alerting and autonomous power backup. This work presents the design and experimental evaluation of an Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT)-enhanced fire and gas detection system built around an Arduino UNO Q dual-processor board. An MQ2 sensor detects combustible gases such as LPG (Liquified Petroleum Gas) and propane, while an IR flame sensor detects fire through infrared radiation in the 700-1100 nm band. An STM32U585 microcontroller performs real-time sensor acquisition, severity classification and alarm actuation, while a Qualcomm Dragonwing QRB2210 processor running Linux handles cloud connectivity and edge-AI inference. Sensor readings are processed by AI-based anomaly detection, a flicker filter that suppresses false positives, and a five-level severity classification, and are sent to the Blynk cloud for real-time remote monitoring. Local alerts are provided by a buzzer, colour-coded LEDs and an OLED display, and a SIM800L GSM module delivers SMS alerts to up to five authorised recipients and supports live room audio monitoring. A USB camera records a one-minute video clip at the onset of a confirmed alarm and stores it on the board and in the Blynk cloud, while an Edge Impulse image classification model labels the scene as person, animal, fire, smoke or background, so that every alert states whether people or animals are present. An 18650 lithium-ion battery with TP4056 charging and MT3608 boost modules sustains approximately fifteen hours of idle operation and eight hours under mixed alarm conditions without mains power. Experimental results confirm reliable detection, prompt alert delivery and uninterrupted operation, demonstrating the system's suitability for residential and light-industrial environments.
evidence_items.title: Design and Experimental Evaluation of an Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT)-enhanced Multi-Modal Safety System

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly applied in forensic accounting to detect fraud, anomalies, and financial risks across large transaction populations. This chapter reviews AI applications in forensic accounting, fraud detection, auditing, and sustainable reporting, with emphasis on detection performance, data requirements, interpretability, and forensic usability. It examines key AI and ML techniques and discusses practical challenges including class imbalance, false positives and negatives, overfitting, data leakage, concept drift, and model validation. The chapter also considers AI-supported verification of (ESG) and (CSR) disclosures and the supporting roles of blockchain and big data analytics. Drawing on the reviewed evidence, it proposes a conceptual framework in which AI-enabled detection contributes to reliable financial and sustainability reporting when supported by data quality, regulatory maturity, auditor expertise, and explainability. The chapter concludes that AI should augment, rather than replace, professional forensic judgment
evidence_items.title: Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence in Forensic Accounting

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has had and will continue to have, an unprecedented impact on higher education. Yet the integration of AI literacy into postsecondary curricula remains rare and inconsistent. Academic librarians, due to their expertise in information literacy and interdisciplinary collaboration, are uniquely positioned to address this gap. This chapter presents a case study of a credit-bearing AI literacy course housed within the academic library at CSUN. The course was designed not only to introduce students to AI but to support the development of epistemic agency, allowing them to critically evaluate AI-generated information, interrogate algorithmic bias, and navigate an AI-mediated information environment. Grounded in the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Students, the Council of Europe's three-dimensional model of AI literacy and ACRL Framework for Information Literacy for Higher Education, the course emphasizes the practical and human dimensions of AI literacy and provides a pedagogical framework that academic librarians can adapt across instructional formats.
evidence_items.title: Critical Thinking in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Purpose of Review Physical activity prevents cardiovascular disease, yet prescriptions remain generalized. This review synthesizes evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) models applied to exercise data for cardiovascular risk prediction, stratification, and outcomes. Recent Findings A literature search across four databases yielded 18 primary studies (PROBAST/TRIPOD-AI evaluated). Deep learning estimated VO₂ peak from resting EKGs. Low predicted fitness was associated with 5-year CVD mortality (AUC 0.83). Neural networks predicted Peak VO₂ ( r = 0.87) from submaximal exercise data. Random forest models applied to treadmill tests predicted 10-year hypertension incidence (AUC 0.93). Machine learning classifiers processing accelerometry associated brief, vigorous lifestyle activity with reduced cardiovascular event risk. Adaptive reinforcement learning increased daily steps by ~ 606/day in a randomized trial. Summary AI shows promise for improving the precision of exercise-based cardiovascular medicine. However, current evidence is retrospective with narrow demographic diversity. Clinical integration requires completing randomized trials powered to demonstrate reductions in hard cardiovascular endpoints. Graphical Abstract Architectural workflow of artificial intelligence in exercise cardiology. Overview of data intake, computational processing, and downstream clinical translational outputs. (A) Data Input Layer: Multimodal continuous and discrete inputs comprising wrist-worn accelerometry, photoplethysmography (PPG) heart rate time-series, 12-lead electrocardiography (EKG), and cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) parameters. (B) Computational Processing Layer: Four core AI paradigms process raw inputs: supervised learning algorithms, deep learning architectures, unsupervised algorithms and reinforcement learning agents.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Exercise and Cardiovascular Disease: A Structured Narrative Review

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The food packaging industry continuously strives to balance the sealing performance, durability, and aesthetics. Because the sealing layer is the most critical component of a multilayer film, polymers are required to design high-performance structures. Ionomers, characterized by pendant ionic groups along the polymer chain, are highly suitable for these applications; however, traditional versions often exhibit performance gaps regarding seal-through contamination. In fact, in many packaging operations, contamination of the sealing layer is inevitable. This study presents a class of polyethylene ionomers based on ion pair comonomers (IPCs) as an alternative to the classic ethylene–methacrylic acid (EMAA) ionomer, known as Surlyn. These E-IPC ionomers are synthesized via the free-radical copolymerization of ethylene with amine-terminated methacrylates and methacrylic acids. The materials were evaluated based on their seal initiation temperature (SIT) and plateau seal strength (PS) in comparison to Surlyn. Experimental results demonstrate that a balance between a low SIT and a high PS can be achieved by tuning the IPC content. Furthermore, while commercial ionomers typically experience a significant drop in performance when contaminated with food particles, the E-IPC ionomers maintained a superior performance in three of the four contamination scenarios explored. These findings position E-IPC ionomers as compelling candidates for sealing layers in advanced packaging applications.
evidence_items.title:

evidence_items.summary: Global benchmark inclusion not only can ease the frictions in the equity-market, but also enhance the information provided to creditors, its impact on corporate leverage is theoretically ambiguous. This essay discusses that ambiguity based on annual firm-level data of 819 listed companies in the Gulf Cooperation Council between 2011–2025 and historical MSCI constituent additions related to the staggered reclassifications of the United Arab Emirates and Qatar in 2014, Saudi Arabia in 2019, and Kuwait in 2020. The comparison of actual entrants with contemporaneous same-country non-entrants is done on the basis of firm and country-by-year fixed effects, dynamic event studies, support restrictions, leave-one-country-out tests, placebo reassignment, and multiple-testing adjustments. The entrants decrease debt/assets by 6.77 percentage points as compared to non-entrants. The trends of the leverage pre-treatment are flat, the downward trend starts in the inclusion year and the difference is about 8.1 percentage points in year +2 and +3. The answer is concentrated in firms that have high leverage before inclusion and is found in multiple definitions of leverage and direct component tests find the adjustment is concentrated in long-term debt with some asset contraction offsetting the leverage decrease. Other alternative +1 to +4 and +3 to +5 window averages do not exhibit expansion significant at 5 per cent, but an isolated year +5 CAPEX increase is sensitive to sample composition. The results indicate that financial integration through benchmarking may result in long-lasting balance-sheet rebalancing as opposed to debt growth, and the direction of adjustment will be affected by the financial structure of the receiving market and initial leverage of firms.
evidence_items.title: When Global Benchmark Inclusion Lowers Corporate Leverage: Evidence from GCC Equity Markets

evidence_items.summary: Microplastic contamination has emerged as an environmental concern in modern agricultural production, including hydroponic systems that are increasingly adopted for their efficient use of water, nutrients, and growing space. This review examines the sources, transport pathways, plant uptake mechanisms, and potential food safety implications of microplastics and nanoplastics in hydroponic agriculture. A structured narrative review of relevant scientific literature was conducted to evaluate the occurrence and behaviour of plastic particles in hydroponic environments, with particular attention to nutrient solutions, growing materials, agricultural infrastructure, and edible crops. The review identifies contaminated source water, degradation of plastic pipes and reservoirs, growing substrates, atmospheric deposition, and maintenance activities as potential pathways through which microplastics enter hydroponic systems. Once introduced, their movement and accumulation are influenced by particle size, polymer composition, surface characteristics, nutrient solution chemistry, and system design. Experimental evidence indicates that certain small plastic particles can penetrate plant roots and, under specific conditions, translocate into aboveground tissues, including edible portions of crops such as lettuce. However, the extent of particle uptake under commercial hydroponic conditions and the associated risks to human health remain insufficiently understood. The review also highlights limitations in existing analytical methods, particularly the difficulty of distinguishing external particle adhesion from internal uptake and the lack of standardized detection procedures. To minimize contamination, the study recommends improved source-water treatment, appropriate material selection, routine system maintenance, effective filtration, and reliable monitoring techniques.
evidence_items.title: MICROPLASTIC CONTAMINATION IN HYDROPONIC AGRICULTURE: SOURCES, TRANSPORT PATHWAYS, PLANT UPTAKE AND FOOD SAFETY IMPLICATIONS

evidence_items.summary: Arabic social-media text is classified at national scale, yet the computing cost of Arabic text classifiers is rarely reported. We benchmark twelve model configurations from five families (sparse linear, fastText, convolutional, recurrent and Transformer encoders, with product-quantized, feature-hashed and INT8 variants) on five Arabic dialectal tasks, with three pretrained Arabic BERT encoders as a reference. All models were trained and profiled on one core of a server CPU at batch sizes from 1 to 512, measuring CPU time end to end and for the model computation alone. Because the host exposes no energy counters, energy is reported as a first-order estimate from CPU time at an assumed 12 W per core. The encoders’ CPU costs are proxy estimates from architecture-matched networks, and neural costs are reported both with inputs padded to 64 tokens and at their true length. Among models trained only on the task data, a character n-gram linear SVM, with exact or hashed features, gave the best macro-F1 on every task (0.407–0.861). fastText was the cheapest model for single requests (0.34–0.52 J per 1000 predictions), 9–15 times below every neural model with padded inputs and 6–9 times at true length, and word-level linear models were the cheapest once requests were batched. Compact neural encoders trained from scratch on word or subword tokens were significantly less accurate than the character SVM on every task and never reached the accuracy–cost Pareto front. The pretrained encoder MARBERT was the most accurate model, 7–12 macro-F1 points above the SVM on four of five tasks, at a proxy cost of 121–198 times the SVM’s CPU time per single prediction (true length to padded). Each additional macro-F1 point it bought cost 47–202 J per 1000 predictions, against 0.55–3.5 J for the reliable steps between lightweight models.
evidence_items.title: Accuracy, CPU Time and Estimated Energy of Lightweight Models for Arabic Dialectal Text Classification: A Single-Core Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: A foundation model for time series is pretrained once and then asked to forecast series it has never seen, so the evidence for it is its score on held-out datasets. Such datasets are scarce, and a few public leaderboards carry most comparisons, yet none of them states how small a difference its datasets can detect. We call that quantity the resolution of a board and introduce Vernier, a tool that computes it from the files a board already publishes. Vernier also reports which entries a board cannot separate from its leader and whether its order changes when unrelated parties submit. GIFT-Eval resolves 6.8 rank places, and its displayed neighbours sit 0.91 apart. The ten places of its top ten hold fewer than two resolvable steps. fev-bench, Chronos Benchmark II and TIME show the same pattern: their resolution is 3.6 to 19 times the gap between neighbours. With each of its 2,554 series as an independent source, BOOM is the one board that resolves its top ten. Below the resolution the order depends on who else submitted: across four boards, rules that rank against the pool reversed 43 top-ten pairs with neither entry rerun, in one update in seven. Boards also do not record how much history a model receives. On 70 configurations, shortening it raised the error of three of four open models, two of them by 15%. We release Vernier, which runs this report with one command on any leaderboard that publishes per-dataset scores: https://github.com/therealram18/vernier
evidence_items.title: What a Forecasting Leaderboard Can Establish: Resolution Reporting for Zero-Shot Time-Series Models
